TUBERCULOSIS MORBIDITY AND MORTALITY IN PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
1.	What has been done under the national health grants program to reduce tuberculosis morbidity and mortality in the province of Quebec?
2.	What reduction has there been in the tuberculosis mortality rate in the province of Quebec, since the inauguration of the national health grants program?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: TUBERCULOSIS MORBIDITY AND MORTALITY IN PROVINCE OF QUEBEC
speechtext:
1.	Since 1948, approximately $7,034,000 has been expended under the federal health grants program for the control of tuberculosis in Quebec. Included is federal assistance amounting to $2,234,000 toward the construction of 2,021 additional beds in nine provincial sanatoria. Preventive, diagnostic and treatment services were provided. Staff and equipment were provided for diagnostic clinics, mobile clinics and sanatoria. Drugs such as streptomycin, para-amino salicyclic acid and tibione were purchased for free distribution to tuberculous patients. A B.C.G. vaccination program among children has been established and various investigations into B.C.G. vaccine were carried out.
2.	The death rate from tuberculosis in Quebec has fallen markedly-in 1950, the rate was 39-3 per 100,000 as compared with 72-4 per 100,000 in 1946.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxlon (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: COMPASSIONATE LEAVE TO ARMED FORCES SERVING ABROAD
speechtext: This question is a very difficult one to deal with. The most serious consideration is given to all requests for compassionate leave. Generally speaking the practice is followed to return a soldier from the front line in Korea when a parent is ill only in cases where the return of the soldier is likely to contribute to the recovery of the parent. Otherwise men would be coming and going, often too late and often to no avail whatever. However, the most serious consideration is given to each case on its merits.

speechtext:
Yesterday the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked a question regarding the report that United States citizens in Canada were being instructed to register at United States consular offices in this country and he inquired

'whether any arrangements had been made with Canada to cover the enforcement of those reported regulations.
I would like to confirm what I said yesterday that there are no such arrangements, and to add that the position of the government had been made clear in this matter by a circular note dated May 6, 1947, which was sent to all foreign missions and consular offices in Canada. The pertinent portions of this circular note, which was based on section 11 of the Foreign Enlistment Act, read as follows:
As indicated in section 11 of the Foreign Enlistment Act there is no objection in principle to a foreign representative sending a call-up notice to a person who is a national of that country and who is not a Canadian citizen. However, the view of the Canadian government, with which foreign representatives will naturally wish to comply, is that such call-up notices should not give the impression that failure to obey will expose the person to penalties on Canadian soil.

should like to direct to the Minister of Transport a question of which I have already given him notice. I should like to know if the statement appearing in an editorial in a recent issue of the Daily News of St. John's, Newfoundland, is correct, namely, that two of the runways at Gander airport necessary for landing and take-off in cross winds cannot be used by the large aircraft now in use on the international routes. Further, I should like to ask if he has any comment to make on the suggestion contained in the editorial that Mr. Chevrier's department would be quite happy to see Gander by-passed and thus be relieved of the obligation for its maintenance.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIRPORTS
subsubtopic: GANDER, NFLD.-CONDITION AND CAPACITY OF AIRSTRIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a few minutes before I came into the house the hon. member sent me the clipping to which he has referred. The article is not only inaccurate but it is untrue. In the first place there is nothing abnormal about not being able to operate aircraft in cross winds on certain strips. There is a main strip at Gander on which the government has spent a substantial sum of money and which is capable of taking any loads and any aircraft which may be used on any occasion. There is absolutely nothing the matter with that airstrip.
It is a fact that the two airstrips referred to have been affected by the frost and we have definite plans for the development of the Gander airport. That is indicated by the fact

that we have already spent several millions of dollars there. We have in hand now a proposal with reference to the town site which we are discussing with the provincial authorities. This is not indicative of our by-passing Gander. Not only are the contents of the article untrue, but quite the converse is the fact.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to indicate once more that I am not opposed to a scheme to provide pensions for members of parliament but I am opposed to the present plan.
My reasons are that I am convinced, as a result of the discussions and the evidence presented in the banking and commerce committee, that the present scheme can and should be modified by way of an age floor and some restrictions on the rights to withdrawal so as still to permit a substantial pension benefit to members while at the same time reducing if not eliminating the proposed level of treasury contributions and thus removing from the scheme those features which, as I see them at present, must subject parliament itself to damaging criticism.
I have pressed these views as vigorously as possible both here and in the banking and commerce committee and from what has followed I can only conclude that my views are not generally shared.

speechtext:
As I recall it, the amendment which was put forward and which was defeated in the committee was to the effect that these agreements or reinsurance contracts between the Minister of Finance and the mutual insurance club of ship owners should contain a provision that there should be a period of 14 days after tabling in the house, within which the agreements could be annulled by joint vote of the House of Commons and the Senate. The Minister of Finance came to the committee and said that such a provision would be quite contrary to the general conception of responsible government; that the government must take responsibility for whatever contracts they may enter into under this legislation, and he pointed out further that should the actual ship owners who were insuring through their mutual insurance company-a bill for which
War Risks Insurance
will be back before this house on Friday night-find later that the contract could be broken unilaterally by action of the house they would probably be a little reluctant to enter into such contracts, and for that reason the Minister of Finance said that the suggested amendment was not acceptable to him, and it was voted down.

subtopic: WAR RISKS INSURANCE
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF MARINE AND AVIATION ACCOUNT
speechtext: Supplementing what the parliamentary assistant has said, I just want to put on record the fact that our view was that this amendment, which was taken from the Emergency Powers Act, was a good one. I want to put on the record that while the Minister of Finance did say that this was unusual-I think the only one instance that he knew of, and that he said was not properly applicable in this case, was the emergency powers provision- while that view prevailed, I just want to state that in our view it was sufficiently important to be adopted. I am not pursuing the matter now but I should like to put on record that we were defeated but not convinced.

subtopic: WAR RISKS INSURANCE
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF MARINE AND AVIATION ACCOUNT
speechtext:
I should like to reinforce what was said by the hon. member for Greenwood and to press one point which was raised in the committee when we asked for a further amendment to the bill.
It is true that the principal section of the bill has been amended with a view to setting forth the purposes for which powers are vested by parliament in the governor in council in respect to insurance for war risks. That goes some distance in meeting the fundamental objection that some of us had to this open type of legislation. When I say "open" I mean that as submitted to the house in the first place it empowered the governor in council without limitation, and without any attempt at setting limits or bounds, to enter into contracts for this type of insurance.
There was one further provision which it seemed to me might well be inserted in the bill with a view to maintaining direct control by parliament over the exercise by the governor in council of the powers vested in him by this legislation. I refer to the precedent provided in this connection by the Emergency Powers Act, chapter 5 of the first session of 1951. There you recall, Mr. Chairman, that following the vesting of certain powers of parliament in the governor in council, parliament saw fit to attach this provision to be found in section 2 subsection 5 of that act:
(5) If the Senate and House of Commons within a period of forty days, beginning with the day on which any regulation is laid before parliament in accordance with subsection four, and excluding any time during which parliament is dissolved or prorogued or during which both the Senate and House

War Risks Insurance
of Commons are adjourned for more than four days, resolve that it be annulled, it shall cease to have effect.
It would not go the whole way, but at least it would be one additional means of maintaining parliamentary control over the exercise by the governor in council of the powers vested in him by this bill if such a provision were written into it. There is a counterpart of such a provision also in the act of the United Kingdom to which frequent reference was made in the committee on banking and commerce, and from which the words were borrowed which have how been written into section 3 of the bill by way of amendment thereto. The mere provision for annulment in terms like these is not of very much effect, Mr. Chairman, unless there is some undertaking and willingness on the part of the government, as there was, you will recall, in connection with the Emergency Powers Act, to make it possible for a private member of the house to introduce one of those motions to annul.
On that occasion the Prime Minister gave an undertaking that even in spite of the difficulties that normally attend the introduction of motions by a private member, every effective opportunity would be given for this purpose if any private member indicated that he wished to bring such a motion under the provisions of section 2, subsection 5, of the Emergency Powers Act. In the case of the present bill, I urge that such an amendment should be written into it and that such an undertaking should be given on the part of the government.
I might point out in that connection also that under the British bill it is sufficient if the House of Commons alone passes a resolution to annul these contracts of insurance. It is not necessary that the resolution be passed by both houses of parliament.
In conclusion, I know I do not need to repeat what I said in the committee in speaking on both these proposed amendments, that there is no quarrel in this house, so far as I know, with providing a means of writing insurance of this kind. The risks are extraordinary and the occasion can descend upon us without warning. We must be prepared; we must take steps in advance to prepare should such unhappy emergency arise. The principle that some of us have seen in this matter, which seems to be directly raised by the wide terms in which the legislation was submitted to the house, is the issue as to how far parliament can go in vesting legislative power in the governor in council. The one amendment to this bill does help somewhat in that respect. I urge on the government again that they agree to a further amendment to the bill which, 
while in itself it is not completely effective, nevertheless has much to be said for it by way of maintaining parliamentary control over the exercise by the governor in council of these powers which the bill will vest in the governor in council.

speechtext: May I be permitted to ask just one question? Will boats such as the ferry steamers Abegweit, Prince Edward Island and the Nova Scotia, and other boats running to Prince Edward Island, be insured, or are they already insured?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: WAR RISKS INSURANCE
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF MARINE AND AVIATION ACCOUNT
speechtext:
Unfortunately I am not
familiar with the ownership of these ships. Are they publicly owned or privately owned?

subtopic: WAR RISKS INSURANCE
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF MARINE AND AVIATION ACCOUNT
speechtext: Two of them are privately owned and two are government-owned.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: WAR RISKS INSURANCE
subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF MARINE AND AVIATION ACCOUNT
speechtext:
As far as the privately-owned ships are concerned, the owners of the ships would decide whether they wanted to come into this Canadian Shipowners Mutual Assurance Company to cover their ships with war risk insurance in the case of hostilities or apprehended hostilities. The experience of the last war shows that private ship owners whose ships were likely to encounter war risks immediately took part in this arrangement.
As far as the government-owned ships are concerned, while they are covered by marine insurance in time of peace they too might be exposed in time of war. It would then be a government decision as to whether those government-owned ships would be placed in the pool or whether they would take the chance directly as the government does with most of its other properties.
As far as the privately-owned ships are concerned, that is a decision for their owners. The experience of the last war shows that if the owners think that there is any war risk involved they would immediately enter the pool.

subtopic: WAR RISKS INSURANCE

346.	Unforeseen Improvements, $1,200,000.

Is this
another way of saying "sundries"? I notice that last year the amount budgeted for was not wholly spent. Last year the amount in the estimates was $2,200,000 and the amount spent was $1,300,000. Could we have some explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This is the second year we have had this estimate, and it is based on past experience in the department. I will read what notes my officials have given me about this vote. This vote is required to cover works of a structural nature for which there is no specific appropriation but which cannot be charged to the maintenance vote under the allotment "repairs and upkeep", such as the installation of new elevators or air conditioning systems, construction of small additions, fire escapes, fences, major repairs such as strengthening foundations, supporting walls or floors, reconstruction of roofs and major ground improvements.
In setting up the new objects of expenditure treasury board took the stand that such works are more controllable and therefore should be distinguished from the ordinary repairs and maintenance and interior alterations required for accommodation of employees. The estimate of $1,200,000 for 1952-53 is based roughly on estimated expenditures for 1951-52. As this vote includes "unforeseen" improvements the actual expenditures will of course vary from year to year depending upon the number of projects that come to light from month to month. The estimated requirements for 195253 are divided, as shown in the details on page 405, as follows: At Ottawa, $300,000; other than Ottawa, $900,000.
The appropriation last year was $2,200,000 of which $1,180,703.14 was spent. That is why we have decreased the amount this year now that we have experience to guide us in the preparation of the estimate. This vote was provided for the first time in 1951-52 when the estimates were submitted in the new setup by "objects". The amount of $2,200,000 was a tentative figure as expenditures for works of this nature for previous years had not been listed separately by the treasury office. The amount of $2,200,000 provided for 1951-52 proved to be considerably greater than the actual requirement. Using 1951-52 expenditures as a guide the estimated requirement for 1952-53 has been placed at $1,200,000 which is a reduction of $1 million compared with the preceding year. This way of presenting the estimates was adopted on the recommendation of the comptroller of the treasury and treasury board. We made these

expenditures before but they came out of a general vote. Treasury board wanted to have this special item so they could exercise a better audit and control over it.

I am not
offering any opinion for the moment whether it enables treasury board to maintain better control, but if I have understood the minister's explanation it seems to me on the face of it that it is rather open to some question. The minister said, for example, that it would enable elevators and fire escapes to be provided as well as the strengthening of foundations and so forth. Would it be fair to say that this amounts to-what shall I say- being able to fix up an estimate which is not working out according to plan? In other words, you have an estimate for a building and you find you need some more money. As I understand it, instead of going back and correcting that, which might present some difficulties, we now begin all over again with a little separate contract. I assume of course it will all be done by tender after our discussions of last autumn, but will the minister say why, from the point of view of the efficient carrying out of an original contract, it is not carried through, and not supplemented by money brought in from a special fund for an elevator, a fire escape or for strengthening a foundation? It may be more convenient from the point of view of treasury board but if I have understood the situation correctly it seems to present certain questions from the business point of view.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps I was not clear enough for my hon. friend. This amount is expended as we go along. When we get reports from our architects and other officials in their districts that buildings are in a condition which they could not foresee when the estimates were prepared, we have to give out a contract for instance to reinforce a foundation.
We follow the same procedure with this vote as with others. We have plans and specifications prepared, tenders called for, and the lowest tender gets the contract. These additional works are not foreseen in the preparation of the estimates. When you have assets in construction as considerable as public works have you cannot think of everything or foresee everything that is going to happen to a building. This was experimented with last year and we had to follow the decision of treasury board. They wanted to have this special vote and follow each project as it goes along. The matter is submitted to treasury board before we can get an allotment to cover these works.
