speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The site was purchased in 1938 from Mr. McLaren for the sum of $6,500. The estimated cost of the building would be $60,000; grading and sidewalks, $1,500; supervision, $2,000; contingencies, $11,500. The contract has not been let and I am not sure but I believe that plans for this building are being prepared in the department although I cannot say at what stage they are.
Since 1938, you see, it has been more or less-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On the rails.
-on the way. I hope the minister will see to it that plans are completed and the contract let at an early date.

The minister says he has no responsibility for the burned up lawns, the dandelions, plantain and other weeds, but would he tell members what minister is responsible for the condition of the grounds surrounding the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly.
I want to compliment whoever is responsible for the beautiful flowers there were and which will be there later this year, but the lawn is disgraceful.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The federal district commission comes under the jurisdiction of the president of the privy council.
Who is he?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, I know I am Minister of Public Works and I know who the president of the privy council is. He is the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent. In so far as these grounds are concerned, I was in the house in 1933 when Mr. Bennett's government thought the federal district commission had the expert people to maintain these grounds. It was thought that we did not have the right people to look after these flowers, lawns, shrubs and all of that. These activities were taken away from our department and handed over to the federal district commission. I think it was a wise move, but ever since the Minister of Public Works seems to bear the load* even though the grounds do not come under his department.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Dredging-
350. Maintenance and operation of plant and contract and day labour works, $3,077,989.

This item has to do with dredging, and I would ask the minister to explain

whether anything is being done about dredging Vancouver harbour during the present fiscal year. There was some discussion on this question when the estimates of the Department of Transport were under consideration, and the minister of that department indicated that, while his department and particularly the national harbours board were very interested in that harbour, any actual dredging would have to be done by the Department of Public Works. I do not need to point out to the minister the great importance of Vancouver harbour. I do not think there is a finer harbour in Canada, possibly on this continent. There is a great deal of traffic going into and out of the harbour.
The situation has now developed that the first narrows, which is the entrance to the harbour, has to be dredged approximately five feet deeper. The necessity for this work has arisen because there are such large oil tankers being built now, which apparently run up to 40,000 tons and over. Some of the tankers are now waiting outside the harbour in order to get the tide at the right stage, although I think that is primarily because of the currents in the second narrows and not the depth of the first narrows. It is agreed on all sides that the first narrows will have to be dredged a further five feet. I am told there has been no dredging there since 1947, which is some five years ago.
This matter is urgent. The dredging will take some time. I hope the Department of Public Works is planning to commence that work during this fiscal year. Unfortunately I cannot find any vote to cover it, either in the regular estimates or in the supplemen-taries, but I believe it is one of the most important works that can be undertaken by the department. I hope the minister will see to it that the work is at least commenced.
Eventually, the first narrows will also have to be widened. There has been a suggestion made by responsible people in Vancouver who are interested in the harbour that a scale model of the harbour should be set up by the dominion government, and the whole question of the future development studied in that way. As the minister knows, there is a model now at the University of British Columbia for studying the currents in the Fraser river. I believe that a similar model for Vancouver harbour, including the first and second narrows, would be very beneficial. It seems this is the modern way of dealing with these harbour improvements. I believe there is such a model, for example, for the development of Niagara falls. I hope the minister will discuss with his colleagues
Supply-Public Works
the possibility of having a model set up and a study undertaken of the whole harbour situation.
But in the meantime this dredging is urgent. I believe the cost of dredging out a further five feet would not be very high. I have an article here from the Vancouver Sun of June 2, by Roy W. Brown, one of our leading journalists in British Columbia, in which he says that this dredging could be done within a year or fifteen months.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Who said that?

Roy W. Brown of the Vancouver Sun. He is one of the senior and outstanding journalists of British Columbia, and has a wide knowledge of harbour conditions. He says he believes the job could be done within a year or fifteen months at a cost of about a million and a half. Can the minister tell us the situation with regard to that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Three bodies are interested in this project, the national harbours board, the Department of Transport and the Department of Public Works. They are actually studying the situation, but I am told the problem is more complicated and the costs would be far more extensive than those mentioned by the hon. member. The idea of having a model, such as the one prepared by national research for the currents in the Fraser river and the former one they had for Niagara falls, seems to be a good one. However, that could not be done in a short time.
That suggestion would be for studying the long term plan. I should like to keep that suggestion distinct from the need for dredging right away.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Before you can undertake the dredging of the first narrows or the enlargement of it, I am told there is need for a whole scheme and specifications to be prepared. These engineers-I am told they are good men in their line of business-are afraid that the effect of doing the work without having a complete plan and specifications or by the piecemeal method of dredging in the first narrows, would be contrary to the effect the hon. member expects from this dredging. This is one of the projects in which the department is most interested, and you may be sure that with the co-operation of national harbours board and the Department of Transport we will keep this in mind and do our best to hasten the execution of the project.
What progress can be made if there is no money in the estimates?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The study of this problem by the engineers of the three departments does not need a special estimate. When we have these plans and specifications we

Supply-Public Works certainly will, but the work will not start this year. That is the information I have. We cannot start dredging without the hydraulic studies that have to be made. I am trying to speak as an expert in this matter, but I am not. When we have a report from these people, and the model they can study, we will certainly make a decision. We will have time to have an estimate submitted to the house before starting the work.

On this question of dredging, in view of the obviously difficult and embarrassing situation with respect to Vancouver harbour, I am sure that the minister is delighted with the fact that we do not have any dredging problems in Halifax harbour. We have, however, some important requirements for dredging in fishing harbours along the coast in Halifax county. I hope that the minister will not permit the necessity of finding a solution to the difficult and expensive problem in Vancouver to delay the important projects that we require on the east coast.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I should like to point out that the amount of traffic handled in Halifax could be easily handled in Vancouver with the present entry to the harbour. What the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and I are thinking about is the great expansion of harbour traffic which will occur when the deep-sea tankers come in to feed off the Trans Mountain oil lines. I hope that this dredging, most of which will be in my riding, will be accomplished within the next year. We expect to see in the estimates of next year a substantial item so that this work can be undertaken in the spring of next year.

The minister has had a year in which to study the dredging requirements in the port of Pugwash in my constituency. He has shown great interest in the requirements there when I have drawn the matter to his attention on various occasions. I see there is an appropriation here of $4,166,989. That is a general appropriation. Then there are several appropriations running into hundreds of thousands of dollars, also for the St. Lawrence river $13 million, $15 million and so on.
At the port of Pugwash we have perhaps as fine a natural small harbour as there is anywhere in Canada, but there is some dredging required there. In recent weeks some of these ships carrying pulpwood, pit props and lumber have touched on the bends of the channel, which again emphasizes the necessity for some dredging. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra says that no dredging has been done in his harbour for five years. No dredging has been done in Pugwash since the beginning of time; but it


is needed in order to improve the channel where there are bends and shallow places. I would ask the minister whether, in the last year, he has been able to give further effective study to the requirements and whether he will hold out any promise of dredging to improve conditions in Pugwash.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The only thing that I recall is this. I believe that two years ago we had some dredging done at Pugwash to the amount of $300,000 or $400,000. Ever since then I had been under the impression that the work was completed to our satisfaction.
That was building a wharf.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Then we will have to have some dredging done.
In order to justify the building of a wharf, you will have to improve the conditions in the channel.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right. I will ask my officials to look into this matter.

Last night I made passing reference to the harbour of Renews. At the harbour of Renews the wharf is not reached easily. It will be necessary to have the place dredged. A firm there is expecting to have a big fish plant, and it will need steamers to go in to the wharf. The whole operation will be held up if the dredging is not carried out. That is the situation as to the wharf. The harbour has been surveyed for dredging and the engineer down there is completely familiar with the situation. The only question is a physical one of getting the dredge to go there. Will there be a dredge available this summer to go to Renews harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot give the exact date on which dredge No. 400 will be in Renews, but I have here a program of dredging with respect to these small harbours in Newfoundland; it will take two or three weeks, using that dredge No. 400, to do the work at Renews.
It will be this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that we have the list of these different places, and that we divide them up into so many days or weeks.
Yes; but will Renews be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am trying to extract that promise from my own officials.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope my hon. friend will not press me too much.
I would remind the minister that I have been at this matter since 1949. I have been three years asking for it.	,
That is a short time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that this is the tenth place on our dredging list in Newfoundland where dredge No. 400 will go and do that work. When it will reach Renews, I do not know; I cannot give an exact date.
That does not seem to me to be fair because it was the first one that was mentioned here. I brought this matter to the minister's attention here on the first estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot say to my officials that it is not fair. The hon. member may say that to me and I will take it; but I do not like to say it to my officials.

I hate to say it, Mr. Chairman, but each year the matter has been brought to the minister's attention and the dredging has not been done. This year there is an annual vote there and it is just a question of getting the dredge.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Locks and dams-
353.	Maintenance and operation, $355,562.
Can the minister explain what type of locks and dams come under the control of his department as distinguished from those which are under the Department of Transport?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This appropriation is required to provide for maintenance and operation of various locks and dams which were built or taken over by this department to raise or maintain water levels of the various lakes and rivers in Canada in the interests of navigation. These locks and dams are in operation during the navigation season. The list of them is as follows: Riviere du Lievre lock and dam, French river dams; Latchford dam; St. Andrews lock and dam; Cowan dam, Okanagan dam; Quinze dam; Timiskaming dam; Fryer's island dam; Lewes river dam. That is the list of the locks and dams that come under my department.
The question I asked is this. Where is the line drawn between the dams and locks which are under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport and those which come under the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
One is under the canal system in the country and this is on the rivers
Supply-Public Works
and lakes where we are responsible for navigation. We administer the Navigable Waters Protection Act and these dams are built not on the canal system which comes under transport but on these rivers and lakes where we are responsible for navigation.
There is quite a substantial increase in the repair and upkeep item which is to be found at page 413. It has gone up by nearly $200,000. Why is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is explained in this way. On the northern part of the Ottawa river, north of Timiskaming there is what they call the Quinze dam which is badly in need of repair. This year we expect to spend $198,886 on that dam. Last year it was only $33,666. That would determine where the increase in work will be done on these dams.

I should like to renew my plea to the minister on behalf of the workmen at St. Andrews lock. I do not think many alterations have been made in conditions there since 1910. Minor regulations may have been changed, but in general they are pretty much the same. As the minister knows, the lock is operated by three lock men and an assistant superintendent. The lock is operated 24 hours a day. Each man works 12 hours. He also works seven days a week. When the men want to change from the day shift to the night shift, they have the swing shift and they work 24 hours a day. I think that situation should be changed. In this day and age we do not ask men to work 12 hours a day. These men, compared with other employees in the government service, are working a day and a half every day. The unfortunate thing about it is that, although they work only seven months a year, during that seven months they put in more hours than the average worker. Then they are laid off, and they find it difficult to get a job in the wintertime. If you take the salaries that they earn per month and divide it up on an hourly rate you will find that it amounts to about 42 cents or 43 cents an hour. That is not a very high wage in these times. The members of the civil service exchange higher salaries for security, but when these fellows are laid off after seven months' work there is no security in the job. Then, they do not have unemployment insurance, and that kind of thing.
On different occasions I have brought this before the minister and he has promised to look into it. I make an appeal now that he do something about it. If you pick up the Canada Year Book and study it you will see that the St. Andrews locks, while small, do a tremendous amount of business. I do not think I am saying anything unreasonable when I say that some of the conditions regarding employment and hours of work in respect to

Supply-Public Works
the locks in the eastern part of Canada should be put into eifect in the St. Andrews locks. I hope that the minister will do what he can for these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am most sympathetic to the representations made by the hon. member and I will discuss it with my officials.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Snagboats-
354.	Maintenance and operation, $113,178.

I should like to say a word on this item and bring to the attention of the minister the work of the snagboats on the Fraser river. At the present time, as I recall it, a snagboat, I think it is Samson V, located at Westminster, is used to remove deadheads and logs from the north arm of the Fraser river particularly. I would draw to the minister's attention the situation that exists in the middle arm of the Fraser river, where apparently sedimentation has now been permitted, and there is no boat traffic through there, but it provides a basin for the airport in respect to seaplanes leaving and arriving at that point. A bad situation exists at that basin at the present time. It is practically loaded with deadheads and presents a dangerous condition for the seaplanes. I rather doubt whether the present Samson can enter the middle channel except at high tide, because of the very low water.
I have already spoken in the house of the very good work being done by private airplane companies. A number of them are running seaplanes out of that basin. They have moved as many as 600 men per day out of there by seaplane. A situation exists there with respect to snags which I think should be remedied. I would ask the minister whether he would pay some attention to the important seaplane base there as well as the general traffic within the north arm of the Fraser and the main arm of the New Westminster to the sea.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Queens.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We have no snagboats in Prince Edward Island. The only snag-boats we have are in the Fraser river. The Samson is employed in the removal of snags and obstructions from the channel of the Fraser river between Chilliwack and the gulf of Georgia, 75 miles. It is also employed in assistance in surveys and inspections and on minor repairs to floats and wharves on the Fraser river and in nearby waters.
The other snagboat, the Essington, keeps the Skeena and Naas rivers, and fishing grounds, clear of snags, floating logs and so
TMr. Bryce.]
forth, which foul and destroy the fishing nets and gear. I will tell my officials to look into the matter referred to by the hon. member.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Roads and bridges-
355.	Maintenance and operation, $321,230.
What roads and bridges come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Public Works?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Burlington channel bridge, that is the one that was struck by a ship not long ago. The Kingston-LaSalle causeway; the New Westminster bridge, and other small bridges; the Great Bear river portage road. I have the list here:	The
Chapeau bridge on the Ottawa river between Allumette island and the mainland; Calumet-Bryson bridge, the Clair bridge in New Brunswick, which is an international bridge; the Des Joachims bridge, on the Ottawa river; the Edmonton-Alberta bridge; I think we have a certain interest in that bridge with the city of Edmonton. That is not a large amount. The city of Edmonton has charge of maintenance and repairs to this bridge. This department, the city and the Canadian National Railways company each bear one-third of the cost of repairs, and that amount of $300 would be our share in the repairs. Then, there is the bridge at Edmund-ston, New Brunswick, and Madawaska, Maine, an international bridge. There is also the Great Bear river, Northwest Territories, Portage road. Then there is the Notre Dame du Nord bridge, that is north of Timiskaming where the Quinze dam is; and the Chaudiere bridge in Ottawa; also the Perley bridge at Hawkesbury, Ontario; Portage du Fort, Quebec; St. Leonard, New Brunswick; Shell-mouth, Manitoba; Matapedia, Quebec, and Missaguash, New Brunswick.
On what basis is jurisdiction given to the minister over bridges? Is it interprovincial and international bridges? What is the basis for providing the jurisdiction?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If the hon. gentlemen has a moment we will look at the British North America Act and we shall try to find the section under which we have the authority. I think it is section 92.
One o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Let me clear this
British North America Act with the hon. gentleman. I do not want to come back to it.

It is subsection 10 of section 92 of the British North America Act which reads as follows:
Local works and undertakings other than such as are of the following classes:
a. Lines of steam or other ships, railways, canals, telegraphs, and other works and undertakings connecting the province with any other or others of the provinces, or extending beyond the limits of the province;
It is under that section that all the provinces want to make me responsible-
I had one in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member
knows about this, because he has been trying to make me responsible for this work. Since confederation these works have been undertaken by the provinces or by the department itself, or the government itself, and then we maintain them.
How does the Edmonton bridge come into that category?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That was at the time when Alberta was a part of the Northwest Territories, years ago before the province was carved out. I suppose that the central government, having jurisdiction over the territories, put up a certain amount of money on that bridge, and now we are paying for the upkeep with the Canadian National Railways and the city of Edmonton.
Is the minister responsible for all bridges in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. Do not give me any more bridges than I need. I understand that the Department of Resources and Development have jurisdiction over those things.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.
356.	Towards international bridge over the St. Croix river between St. Stephen, N.B., and Calais, Me., the state of Maine to pay a like amount (revote), $10,000.

This is a revote toward the survey of the international bridge between St. Stephen, New Brunswick, and Calais, Maine. This bridge is known as the gateway to the maritime provinces. A short time ago the deputy minister visited the particular area and was able to obtain firsthand knowledge of conditions so far as the international bridge is concerned. There is an enormous amount of traffic over the international bridge and it is increasing year by year. Although there is a very efficient staff there, the lack of proper facilities greatly
Supply-Public Works
slows up the examination of freight. In addition all the bus traffic passing through to the west goes through Calais, Maine, and St. Stephen as well as the bus traffic going through to Montreal.
The big problem so far as freight is concerned is the trailer trucks which bring in fruit in particular from the United States to all parts of the maritime provinces. The bridge, which was built in the horse and buggy days, is too small to take care of the traffic that has developed over the years. Although we realize there is a shortage of steel which is responsible for the delay in bringing about this improvement, we are looking forward to the day when the steel supply may be more plentiful so that the department, together with the appropriate United States department, can go ahead with the construction of what is considered to be a very necessary improvement to speed up the handling of tourist and freight traffic entering the maritime provinces. I know the minister is aware of the condition and when the steel situation improves will do what he can to look after it.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
357.	Towards interprovincial bridge over the Ottawa river between Pembroke, Ontario, and Allu-mette island, Quebec, the provinces of Ontario and Quebec each to pay one-third of the cost and maintenance thereof (revote), $50,000.

This bridge is similar to one which we have asked the minister to consider between Campbellton and Cross Point. I should like to ask the minister what the situation is with reference to the request of the residents of the Campbellton and Cross Point districts with respect to the construction of this bridge. Has there been any agreement between the federal government and the two local governments concerned, and has responsibility for the building of the bridge been definitely settled? The minister will remember that last year the matter came up and the premier of New Brunswick was of the opinion that it was the responsibility of the federal government to construct the bridge. I believe the premier of Quebec was also of the same opinion. I noted that just before the recess the minister read a section of the British North America Act. I think it was under that section that the premier of New Brunswick believed it was the responsibility of the federal government. Has anything more been done, and has any agreement been made with the provinces concerned as to the construction of the bridge?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The difference between the two projects is that the one mentioned in this item of the estimates is a bridge to

Supply-Public Works Morrison island on the Ottawa river between the province of Quebec and the province of Ontario. The province of Ontario has agreed verbally at least to build one-third of the bridge. There will be three bridges joining these islands. The province of Quebec has written that they will co-operate but no definite answer has been received. In the case of the proposed bridge between Camp-bellton and Cross Point, the two provinces say that it is not their responsibility and they will not make any contribution.
Has the federal government definitely decided that it is not the responsibility of the federal government?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not go that far and have to have the justice department give any legal advice. So far as the Camp-bellton and Cross Point districts are concerned, however, in order that they will not suffer I believe a ferry service is to be established under the maritime commission between the two places, and I understand that the boat is being constructed at the present time.
Is that to be a temporary measure?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It may be temporary, but how temporary I would not know.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Acquisition, construction and improvements of harbour and river works-
Construction, acquisition, major repairs and improvements of, and plans and sites for, harbour and river works listed in the details of the estimates, provided that treasury hoard may increase or decrease the amount within the vote to be expended upon individual listed projects-
359.	Nova Scotia, $3,401,000.

This is quite an important vote so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned. Some of these appropriations appear to be just token ones giving hope to the communities concerned. I have a quarrel with the minister and his department respecting the item of $150,000 for repairs and improvements to the Brooklyn breakwater in Queens county. Tenders were called for this work earlier in the season and three tenders were received. The lowest tender was that of MacDonald and Mclsaac in the amount of $165,000. The next lowest was that of the Tidewater Construction Company in the amount of $178,000. These are both Nova Scotia firms. The highest tender was from T. C. Gorman and Company in the amount of $192,000. I am particularly interested in this breakwater even though it is not in my constituency. The tender of MacDonald and Mclsaac called for the use of Wallace stone at a price of $27,000 below


the highest tenderer. Wallace stone has been used for breakwaters, bridges and seawalls for one hundred years and more. It has been used in the biggest works in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia.
There is no question as to the quality of the stone produced at the Wallace stone quarries in Cumberland county. The fact that the lowest tender envisaged the use of Wallace stone at a very much lower figure warranted the contract being given to MacDonald and Mclsaac. Instead of that being done new tenders were called for from those who had submitted tenders, and instead of the contract being given to the lowest tenderer in the first instance it was given to the highest tenderer, Gorman and Company, a concern owned by interests in central Canada. Their second price was $57,000 below their original tender.
The only change called for in the new specifications was that, instead of using heavy Wallace stone or local granite, concrete blocks were specified. There were only 3,500 yards of these blocks for the outer face called for, but the contractors were allowed to tender and reduce their prices on the whole structure by $57,000 for only 3,500 yards. This means they had the advantage of the prices quoted by both the other Nova Scotia contractors and were able to reduce the price by that amount, using concrete blocks as against native stone.
Anyone in the construction business or any engineer will be able to substantiate the statement that concrete blocks will not stand the erosion of sea water the same as granite or Wallace stone. Wallace stone, as I have said, has been used for this purpose for hundreds of years and the work has always stood up. Cement is in short supply. When I left Nova Scotia a few weeks ago there was a scarcity of cement with a warning that it would be even scarcer as the season advanced.
The Canadian National Railways need the revenue. I think their rate on transporting Wallace stone from Cumberland county to the Brooklyn breakwater would be $2.25 per ton. Instead of paying the Canadian National Railways $15 million or more on deficit, or refinancing their capital structure, they should be given an opportunity to earn money such as for transporting Nova Scotia stone, rather than use cement to make the composite material for these protective blocks required on the outside of the breakwater.
There is little employment at the present time at Wallace. The workmen have no war industry there and they have no major construction work at the present time and they need employment. It is my opinion, it is

their opinion, and it would be the opinion of engineers generally that artificial concrete blocks cannot be justified in place of natural stone-Wallace stone or local granite.
Contractors from outside Nova Scotia were given advantage over local contractors. They were given the advantage of knowing the prices quoted by these local contractors. The workmen in Nova Scotia, the workmen at Wallace, are denied the opportunity to quarry this stone in a community where there is no defence construction employment whatever. There is a real grievance, Mr. Chairman, and I think if the minister would examine into the whole situation he would agree with me that a mistake was made by the department in giving this contract to central Canadian contractors, and giving them the privilege of using artificial blocks made out of cement when cement is in short supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am grateful to the hon. gentleman for bringing up this case. For years he has been one of my best advisers on works in Nova Scotia and I consider his opinion very highly but this is one of those cases where my department and I thought we could make some economies.
In 1950 in the department we had an estimate prepared for this breakwater. The estimate was $150,000. We called for tenders on June 28, 1950, and I think stone was to be used in the breakwater-Wallace stone or perhaps granite. Two tenders were received -the lowest was $284,459.36; the highest was $305,589.20. My engineers were astounded at the high cost of using Wallace stone or granite for this breakwater but they held off for another year. We did not close at that price as we thought they were exorbitant tenders. On September 5, 1951, we called for new tenders. Only one bid was received- $273,484. That was still a very high price. The third time we called for tenders seriously was on November 21, 1951. We received bids ranging from $165,000 to $192,531. Well, that was still over and above our estimate and the engineers looking into the necessity of the breakwater and the quality of the materials going into it advised having the breakwater built of cement blocks so we changed the specifications and called for new tenders. We received three tenders, the lowest being $135,555.55 and the highest $152,200.
I realize that the breakwater will not be made out of Wallace stone but out of cement. My officials say that the life of this cement will compare favourably with stone if you consider the price which is paid-and we thought we would save quite a bit of money by building it that way. I think we were right there. I like stone-Wallace stone-
Supply-Public Works
myself, but when it became a luxury to use it on a breakwater I thought we should use other means.
With respect to those who did tender I am told that the lowest tenderer has his office in Halifax and that would be in the province of Nova Scotia. The first one was T. C. Gorman and Company. The second one was Tidewater Construction, another Halifax firm tendering at a figure of $148,408; and R. K. MacDonald and Ronald Mclsaac are also in Halifax. So, the three bidders have their offices in Halifax in the province of Nova Scotia.
Now I know these Nova Scotians extend their activities outside the province and we meet them all over the country. They are very aggressive contractors and although they may have offices elsewhere I am told these are three good firms in the province of Nova Scotia.
You can compare this contract for $135,000 with the $305,000 which was the highest tender we received on the first demand for tenders. Perhaps I should have stuck to Wallace stone; I do not know; but my officials would not meet my views. The hon. gentleman knows we have spoken about this matter before. I understood the situation and that this stone was to come from the province of Nova Scotia. It should be put on certain things and they get certain preference for their works, but this amount was too large and I could not comply. I hope the next time we do put up a breakwater we will get tenders with Wallace stone at lower prices.

I appreciate what the minister has said but I cannot agree that there is justification for using concrete blocks. I cannot agree with him that there is justification for giving the successful contractor, who may have an office in Halifax but the firm is not controlled in Nova Scotia, the advantage of the knowledge of the tenders of the other Nova Scotia firms. The lowest tender for the Wallace stone was $165,000, which showed a saving of $27,000 over the tender first submitted by this firm who was finally given the contract at $135,000.
Under those circumstances, it is my opinion it would have been only fair to allow the two Nova Scotia firms who tendered, the Tidewater Construction Company, who tendered for $148,000, and the MacDonald and Mclsaac Company, who tendered for $152,000, to meet the final figure. Neither of these firms recommended concrete blocks for this work. Perhaps they would have accepted the contract at the low figure of $135,000. There was no justification for that reduction

Supply-Public Works
because of the change made in the specifications by the minister or his department. I think everyone will agree with me on that. This outside firm may have had inside information-

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think you are fair in that.
-which the other two firms in Nova Scotia did not have.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wish to deny that. No information was given. We changed the specifications from Wallace stone to concrete blocks. Those specifications were in the requests for tenders. We gave out no information. That is another charge against the officials of my department. You name the man who gave out the information, and I shall attend to him.
I do not want to get any man into trouble. He is in enough trouble now.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a further innuendo; I do not think that is fair to the official. If you know him, give me the name. If you do not want to give it publicly, give it to me afterwards and I shall have an investigation made.

I do not intend to give any name. I think the minister has a lot of good officials, but I think they made an error, perhaps under pressure and perhaps not. I think they made an error in changing the specifications. I am making this statement, that twenty years from now the concrete blocks will not have stood up as the natural stone would have against the washing of the sea.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps you are right that the stone would have a longer life than the cement. I have seen stone in Nova Scotia deteriorate in certain of my buildings. I have to rebuild one right now, and it is of Wallace stone. This company with which we are signing the contract is the T. C. Gorman (Nova Scotia) Limited.

Who are the
shareholders?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not know. If I had to go into who holds the shares of all the companies with whom we do business, we would have to extend our staff because the public works department does business with nearly every large firm in the country. You may be right about the life of the stone and the cement, but on the other hand I think I am right about the price. Any other information you can give me I should like to have, because if I have an official in the branch of engineers who gives out information, I want to know it.
(Mr. Black (Cumberland).]

There is some other additional information I should like to have. There is the work at Diligent river, which is necessary. Perhaps the minister would give me some information with respect to the revote. There was $21,000 last year and $15,000 is provided this year. How much work was done on the Diligent river wharf repairs last year, and is the vote now being requested to complete that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What was the name of that place?
Diligent river, the wharf repairs, $15,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This revote is required to complete the contract with Walker and Hall Limited, at $17,008.66 for repairs to the older portion of the wharf which is badly deteriorated and unsafe for public use. These repairs are necessary to ensure sufficient space for the shipment of pulpwood and lumber, which have an annual value of $120,000.
The work will consist of reconstructing the older portion of this wharf by building two native timber pilework sections 20 feet wide by 71 feet long and 20 feet wide by 85 feet long. These two sections are to be at right angles to each other and the area behind them filled and the surface gravelled. By order in council dated November 12, 1951, authority was granted to enter into a contract with the lowest tenderer, Walker and Hall Limited, of Box 1152, Halifax, Nova Scotia, for wharf repairs at Diligent river, amounting to about $17,008.66. The lowest tender was that of Walker and Hall at $17,008.66, and other tenders were received from R. A. Douglas, K. J. Cochrane, Urquhart Construction Limited, B. A. Allaby and R. P. McLeod.

I raise no objection to the letting of this contract. I am simply inquiring as to whether the amount provided would finish the work as it should be finished. There is no question about the desirability of this work being completed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told it is to complete the job.

There is one other item about which I should like to inquire, and that is the repairs to the wharf at Wallace, $55,000. This is an important community, and there has been a wharf there for many years. I am doubtful as to whether this appropriation will be sufficient to give this place the facility that is warranted by the importance of the community and the amount of shipping using the facilities. I should like to find out from the minister when the work is expected to be completed, and whether tenders have yet been called. If not, when will they be called?

speakerposition: topic
Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This work is to consist of widening the wharf to 40 feet from end to end, including the stone-filled approach, and it includes repair of the existing 311 foot outer timber section by construction of creo-soted pile trestle work driven through the old cribwork. The estimated cost in this case is $55,000. Tenders will be called in the near future and the lowest tenderer will get the contract. I understand this work is necessary for the fishermen loading and landing their fishing gear and landing and shipping live lobsters for delivery by large refrigerator trucks. The work requested by the fishermen consists of widening the existing public wharf, construction of an ell, 250 feet long at its channel end, and dredging the berths on either side of the wharf to 6 and 8 feet respectively. I think tenders will be called in the near future.

I thank the minister. There is no question about this work being justified and warranted. My only doubt is whether the amount provided is sufficient to build the wharf and to make the repairs that are warranted by the freight traffic that uses that wharf.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
360.	Prince Edward Island, $1,950,000.

This item is for harbour improvements, wharves, et cetera for the whole province of Prince Edward Island. A number of votes for new construction work- and they have been generous ones-have gone to Souris and Summerside. Of this fact I have no complaint whatsoever to make. Once again I wish to draw to the attention of the Minister of Public Works the fact that in Charlottetown we were promised a thorough survey of the harbour and its requirements under the Duncan commission. Their recommendation of 1926 has never yet been carried out with regard to Charlottetown harbour improvements. As they promised this survey, I should like the minister to see that we get a survey of Charlottetown harbour this year.
A partial survey was made a few years ago and they commenced making improvements at the east end of the harbour. There is a fair vote for that purpose this year. They are doing an excellent job of it. The whole harbour should have this survey and we should know what we are going to get.
There is one vital thing which we must get there, namely the marine railway slip. This is another unfulfilled promise of two different governments. We have the best location for it, and it would be the means of giving employment to our labour who have to go abroad looking for employment in the railway slip business and so on. For
Supply-Public Works
instance, at the present time we have there machine shops capable of doing the very best work in connection with repairs on steamers, but they cannot go below the water line. We are therefore handicapped in getting contracts even at the present time. We have, however, a couple of contracts from the defence department; that work is all for repairs above the water line. I wish the Minister of Public Works would be serious about this matter and give our harbour a survey this summer. Then we can realize whether or not we are going to have the fulfilment of these promises.
As to the marine railway slip, we would not have large ships any more than our own; but if we just had our own boats to repair and to overhaul, we would haye sufficient work for our labourers and mechanics. We have the mechanics to do the work. For instance, in 1940 when the Charlottetown was lost, if we had had a marine railway slip we would not have lost that steamer. She was on her way to another yard to be overhauled. All of our local boats could be repaired there. At the present time they must go to Pictou, Saint John, Halifax, or Sorel, entailing greater costs. We could have a certain amount of repairs done during the summer season and also during the winter season on the boats that are in the service such as the Brant, the Sorel and others. In addition to that, we would be holding our own people and giving employment to at least 250 men per year.
I want the minister to be serious about this matter and to give it consideration. I am quite grateful for the harbour improvements that have already been started at the eastern end of the harbour, but we must have a survey here; we must have the recommendation of the Duncan commission carried out because it was their commission and they promised to fulfil the recommendations of that commission. This is one that I have been harping on here for six or seven years. Nothing much has been done about it, except that it comes up at every election. I suppose it will come up at this next one and will be promised all over again.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
While I am always ready to try to fulfil promises made 26 years ago, when I was a young man, I am nevertheless surprised that the hon. member raises this matter today; because from 1930 to 1935, when we both were sitting in the House of Commons, I do not know why he did not get these promises fulfilled. That was the time when he could have had these promises fulfilled. I would not be ready

Supply-Public Works right today to make that promise. I certainly admire the patience and tenacity of my hon. friend. For some years past he has been asking me for various works. If we look at the details we find there is an amount shown for Rustieo harbour, breakwater repairs, Rustico harbour landing, a revote; that is in his riding. This year I see we have nearly $100,000 in the estimates for that harbour. It took my hon. friend a few years to convince us that we should do these works. Now we are doing them. I thought we would have a respite of at least this year before he would bring me into a survey of the whole Charlottetown harbour. I see that for Charlottetown we have $375,000 in the estimates.
I recognize that fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is for wharf reconstruction and improvements. I like to listen to my hon. friend but I cannot do everything at the same time. I cannot put up his building, his wharf and attend to his Rustico harbour all at the same time. He and I will be here for a long time yet; and as time goes on he will probably succeed in getting far more than he has obtained up until now.

I should like to ask the minister about one or two items in the Prince Edward Island estimates. The first is with regard to the Souris breakwater repairs. I happen to have been working in the Wallace quarry quite a few years ago getting $50 a month as foreman. In that period we supplied the stone for the Souris breakwater, and for that at Summerside and other places. There is here an appropriation of $101,000, following an appropriation of $86,000 for breakwater repairs at Souris. Can the minister give us some information with regard to what is expected to be accomplished by that expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: This vote is to reconstruct the 406 foot section, 40 feet wide, adjoining the outer block of the breakwater, on the existing creosoted substructure. Work will consist of closed face timber crib, stringers, plank deck, and ballast fill. All timber except the plank deck is to be creosoted. The estimated cost is $101,000. We did work in 1951-52 up to $86,000 on this breakwater. We will be asking for tenders for this new work during the summer or the fall.
I did not understand the minister to say how much rock is required for facing this breakwater.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have not the specifications, but it will be rock fill.
It is to be rock fill?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They say they have plenty of rock on the island.

They have plenty of rock on the island, but any rock that I have seen on Prince Edward Island did not have a very long life. However, I am not going to say anything against it. There are two works here, Wood Island, breakwater extension; that is where the ferry is working under subsidy, and then Tignish, repairs to breakwaters. What is proposed at Wood Island? A great many tourists cross over at Wood Island. So far as the ferry steamers are concerned, they are reasonably good. They are not up to the requirements of the traffic, and the facilities, the wharf and the breakwater are certainly not adequate. I should like a statement from the minister as to what is proposed to improve the facilities.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Construction of 200-foot extension at inner end of the east breakwater, extension to be a tied-back wall of close piles, wales, triangular fillers and galvanized wire rope ties. All timber to be creosoted. The estimated cost of the work is $18,500.

Can the minister give me some information with respect to Tignish, repairs to breakwater on Prince Edward Island? Have tenders been called? If so, who are the successful tenderers? What is the amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Proposed work and estimated cost to rebuild a 573-foot section of the south breakwater with creosoted piles, wales and sheeting, $40,000. That will be by contract. Tenders will be called. By day labour, to repair 115 feet of north breakwater at $8,000.
Has the contract been called for that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think the contract is let. Perhaps the tenders have been called for it, but I cannot recall having signed any.

Can the minister give me information later as to whether tenders have been called and whether a contract has been let? Can he give me information as to who the tenderers are and who put in the lowest tender?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that tenders have been called, but the date for having them in has not expired yet-and I cannot recall the date.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.

361.	New Brunswick, $2,755,000.

I want to ask the minister a general question on this item. It is gratifying to know that great improvements are to be made in the different breakwaters in the province of New Brunswick. I notice that that is also true of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. Is it the general policy of the government to give special attention to these breakwaters?
Yesterday I heard the minister say, in reply to the hon. member for St. John's West, that one at Chance Harbour had been recommended by the Minister of Fisheries. With respect to the repairs to breakwaters throughout the maritime provinces, are the repairs being made as the result of recommendations from the Minister of Fisheries? If so, we feel grateful to the Minister of Fisheries because for many years we had a minister of fisheries in Canada who came from New Brunswick and we never received so much attention with respect to breakwaters as we are having at the present time. Is there a general policy now of improving all breakwaters in the maritime provinces? Are contracts being let for all these different improvements at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: When requests come in for new work or for large repairs to these breakwaters and piers we consult the Department of Fisheries. They have their officials travelling around the coast, and they know the needs of the fishermen. We do not always base our decisions on what they say, but they serve as advisers to public works. When we have to repair these breakwaters our own engineer makes that survey and he makes his report and we act on his report.
The original recommendation comes from the Department of Fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would not say that. We consult them. They are our consultants, but requests come from everybody with regard to these works, from members of parliament, from the mayors, from the fishermen, from the co-operatives and so on, and then we get a report from our own engineer, and to complete the file we do consult the Department of Fisheries, and when the works are not needed, well, we hesitate before undertaking them, but usually these works are needed.
I understood the minister to tell the hon. member for St. John's West yesterday that recommendations with respect to Chance Harbour, for instance, came from the Minister of Fisheries.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No, the request came from the local people, and then we submitted
Supply-Public Works
it to the Department of Fisheries. They inquired and they made a recommendation for it.

Has the minister a recommendation from the inspector of fisheries and the Minister of Fisheries with respect to the petition in Pugwash, Wallace and Malagash for wharves and breakwaters to give protection to the lobster fisheries in that section exposed to the storms of the Northumberland strait? I am. sure the inspector of fisheries would be in accord with requests for sea protection and wharves to serve lobster fishermen in those areas. Has the minister any recollection of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot recall having received it, but I will look it up and if there are recommendations from fisheries they will certainly be consfeered, as the recommendation made by my hon. friend will.

It has been suggested that the recommendations come from the Department of Fisheries with respect to breakwaters and so on. In my experience in the short time I have been here the Department of Public Works gets information that would be available from the Department of Fisheries as to the number of boats that fish out of the many ports that we have in the maritime provinces. That is information which is helpful, and it is information which I know the department makes available to the Department of Public Works. It has to do with the number engaged in fisheries in a particular port where a breakwater is erected and where improvements are asked for, the value of the fishing carried on and the protection that is required to take care of the fleet.

362.	Quebec, $5,165,600.

I should like to say a few words on this item, and I shall speak French on the subject matter.
(Translation):
In the details of this item I see at page 423 of this book of estimates that an amount has been provided for the restoration of the wharf at Ste. Angele, which happens to be located within the constituency I am privileged to represent in this house.
I wish to take advantage of this opportunity to express my appreciation to the government, to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) who have agreed to accept my representations regarding this wharf. This new wharf will be of immense value to the people of Nicolet-Yamaska and Lotbiniere counties and also to several neighbouring

Supply-Public Works constituencies. Moreover, on the other side of the river, the city of Three Rivers, which is located opposite Ste. Angele, will also derive great advantage from this wharf. (Text):

363.	Ontario, $5,609,000.

With respect to this item for Ontario, I see by the details on page 424 that there is an item of $32,000, which is a revote for Goderich harbour and an estimate of $118,000. There is an ^timated $118,000 .to be spent there. Will the minister tell me what is contemplated in that vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
This amount of
$118,000 is to provide for the following: to complete urgent repairs to a portion of the mooring wharf and east harbour wall, $11,000; to reconstruct a 500-foot section of the south pier in steel sheet piling and reinforced concrete, $107,000; making a total of $118,000. The appropriation in 1951-52 was $153,000. Estimated expenditure on Canadian Dredge and Dock Company contract for reconstruction of sections of north and south piers, $113,000; day labour, $8,000, making a total of $124,484.93 including inspection, etc.
Has any consideration been given to moving one of the piers toward the mouth of the river in order to provide more protection?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am told by my
deputy that he does not recall any request being made to move piers. I would not want to be definite, but that is the information given to me.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
365.	Saskatchewan, Alberta and Northwest Territories, $148,500.

Would the minister check the possibility of having a wharf built at Pigeon Lake in Alberta. This wharf was originally constructed in 1935 or 1936 by piling up some rocks and placing a wooden walk on top. Whenever the ice broke up it came up under the platform and then there was nothing left but a pile of rocks. This creates a hazard, not only to those having boats there but to people using the wharf. A number of boats have been broken up on the rocks during the last few years and I cannot understand why some child has not been either seriously injured or killed by falling on the rocks. I

am not asking the minister for an opinion right now, but I urge him to look into the matter and see if something cannot be done.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I shall certainly do that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
366.	British Columbia and Yukon, $6,992,000.
Does the minister consider the dredging equipment now in British Columbia adequate for the needs?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am told that we have three dredges working on the coast in British Columbia, and probably if we had a fourth we could find work for it.
You are considering the construction of another one?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is right.

I should like to refer to repairs to wharf and breakwater and improvements at Sidney, British Columbia. As the minister knows, I am always extremely conservative in my requests to the department. I thoroughly investigate each one before I make a recommendation and therefore I approach this matter with a great deal of confidence. What improvements are envisaged in connection with this important wharf, and when may we expect to have tenders called for the work?

speechtext:

required to effect repairs to the wharf and breakwater, to extend the wharf and to construct a float. The proposed work and estimated cost is as follows:

There are four Vancouver items on page 427, the first being False creek fishing harbour, $100,000, which apparently is a revote. Could the minister state whether anything has been done on this project? Then there is an item of $32,000 for Marpole wharf; another item for $55,000 for the seaplane landing at Sea Island, which is also

a revote, and then finally an item of $35,000 for continuation of sea wall, Stanley park. I presume that that is the yearly contribution that is made. I know this work has been under way for some years. Could the minister give us some information concerning these four votes?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In the case of False creek, this project has been delayed owing to the difficulty in acquiring the necessary site, and opposition from interests presently operating there. Steps have been taken to acquire the land from the Squamish Indians through the Indian affairs branch of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Before the land is purchased it must be appraised and this is being done by the Vancouver real estate board who have been held up by the presence of snow over the area in question. That was the condition when the report was made. The difficulty there is that we must have the land before we can proceed.
Do I understand the minister to say that the Indian affairs branch is going to pay the Squamish tribe for this land?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If we buy the land, probably public works will have to pay.
What amount is involved?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Vancouver real estate board are handling this for us.
Will construction be started during the present fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I could not give an answer as to the date, when we have not acquired the site.
Have any plans been drawn?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
No plans have been prepared as yet. We must have the site and the location before we can deal with the plans.
The next vote the hon. member asked about was that in reference to Marpole wharf. Contract plans were prepared but as they embraced a larger area than the original wharf and overran the boundaries of foreshore property allocated to the department, it has been necessary to negotiate with persons having rights on the adjoining foreshore areas before reconstruction of the wharf can proceed. It is anticipated that these legal matters will be settled in the near future and than we will be able to proceed.
The next item has to do with Sea Island. An order in council dated April 10, 1952, granted authority to enter into a contract with the lowest tenderer, the Vancouver Pile Driving and Contracting Company Limited, of 910 Dominion Bank building, Vancouver, for the construction of a seaplane landing at
Supply-Public Works
Vancouver, Sea island, amounting to $58,275. The highest tender was that of the Todd Construction Company Limited in the amount of $71,337.36. That work is proceeding or will proceed because the tender has been let.
There is enough money in the vote to complete that work?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We are asking for $55,000. I see the lowest tender was $58,000, so we will have to find that money somewhere.
On the preceding page there is an item, "North Vancouver, Burrard inlet, to take over and enlarge harbour, $89,000". What is that?

subtopic: ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES RESPECTING CURRENCY, THE MINT AND THE EXCHANGE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it gives
me a great deal of satisfaction to be able, for the first time, to commend the minister's financial policy. In this bill the Department of Finance quite clearly indicates that it is taking definite steps toward a realistic financial system. A realistic financial system may be described or defined as one which is capable of making, in a community, what is physically possible financially possible.
Anyone who has given any serious thought to the present financial system must have realized time and again that the present system is utterly unable to make what is physically possible financially possible. As a matter of fact, when we get enough goods to make it positively certain that we ought to get on wonderfully well and have plenty of prosperity, then we are in danger of pitching into a depression in which everybody suffers. This fact indicates quite clearly that the

Finance Acts
financial system we now operate under is utterly deficient when it comes to rendering financially possible what is physically possible.
This bill is extremely hopeful in that it indicates quite clearly that the Department of Finance and the Minister of Finance definitely recognize that the thing which gives money value is not gold. For generations people have been taught in school, from the hustings, by the bankers and by every other means of instruction that it is gold behind money that gives money value. Not until 1933 was our country courageous enough to suspend the gold redemption clause and in effect announce that from that time forward the value of Canada's money did not depend upon the capacity of anyone to redeem our money in gold.
This present act aims at suspending the parts of the Bank of Canada Act which indicate that there is virtue in gold as a means of giving value to money. In doing this, by implication our finance department is acknowledging that what give money value are goods and services in a community.
That has been the case all along. Money made of pure gold, studded with diamonds, would soon lose its value in a community where there were not sufficient goods to spend the money on and in which there were not resources enough to produce more goods as fast as those goods were consumed. Thus it has been true all along that the real value of money depended upon the things in the community upon which to spend the money.
This amendment, which we are going to be considering before long, quite definitely confesses that the value of Canada's money from this time forward is going to be recognized as dependent upon goods and services. After all, money is only a medium of exchange. It is only a claim to goods. It is only a title to goods. It can be created readily by any agent with authority to create it whenever there is need for further mediums of exchange or claims to goods.
I am thankful that the minister is able to come before the House of Commons, before I leave it, with a measure which acknowledges this first great fundamental truth about money. Just as soon as we all recognize that the value of money depends on the goods and services in a community and that therefore the amount of money which a community can have and use in active circulation in the community depends upon the amount of goods and services the community has to exchange, then we are in a position to make what is physically possible in terms of goods and services and productive capacity financially possible in terms of the money counter

we use whether it be dollar bills, bank credit or whatever other medium we choose to employ.
There are three more fundamental financial principles which sooner or later a minister of finance in this House of Commons will come forward and concur in or endorse. The first of these three, that is the second great principle of a realistic financial system, is this: Money is just as sound when it is created and spent into circulation as it is when it is created and lent into circulation as practically all our money now is. Unfortunately in this act-probably not by design but because of the nature of it-that important principle is not even implied. Notwithstanding the fact that we are no longer to be relying upon gold as a backing, all our money still is to be borrowed into circulation, the assumption being that the only kind of money that is really sound is money that someone borrows from a bank. While the Bank of Canada will create the money without it necessarily having gold backing, it will not spend the money. If the government wants to use the money, it will have to borrow from the Bank of Canada or from some other bank. This principle is a trammel; it is a handicap; it stands in the way of a realistic financial system. Until a government, a parliament and a people recognize that when there is need for more purchasing power by reason of the amount of goods and services in the community to be exchanged, the government under suitable circumstances can create money debt-free and spend it into circulation to the extent to which it can balance consumption with production we shall and can never have a realistic financial system, that is a financial system capable of rendering what is physically possible financially possible. I do not propose to ask the minister to tell whether or not he agrees with this second principle of government-created debt-free money to be spent, not lent, into circulation. It is one step beyond the distance he is prepared to go; but I am glad that he is acknowledging the first principle.
The third principle of a genuinely realistic financial system is this: It is possible to take the money which is created, debt-free, and use that money to establish a stable price structure both for consumption and production, thereby stabilizing an economy. If a government does not employ that concept it is impossible for it to take adequate care of its price structure within a country; and adequate care in respect of a price structure must be taken, as everybody recognizes. If for instance, just as soon as we begin to get too many hogs in the country, the price of hogs goes down, then obviously we are

disrupting the economy and injuring it. We must be in a position to maintain a stable price for hogs or for any other commodity without subsidizing overmuch. That can be done. We want a stable price at the desired level, whatever that may be found to be; we must not have* a considerable fluctuation in price, a rising and falling, which wrecks people who enter into production, as it is doing now in the Canadian economy, with most deplorable results not only for the present but for the future.
Having established the principle that money depends on goods and services for its value, that the amount of money therefore which you can have in a community depends upon the amount of goods and services you have in the country; having agreed that it is sound for a government under suitable circumstances to create money debt-free and spend it into circulation; and then having learned that a government can use that debt-free money to establish a stable price structure, you must recognize and accept the fourth principle of realistic finance, which is this: A government can use this debt-free money and put it in the hands of the people in such a way that they can buy the products your producers can produce, thereby providing them with a market. I do not propose to go any further into detail in respect of this matter. I do not think it would be quite in order, especially at the present time; but I rejoice that the minister has made the first great step, and I am telling him, the House of Commons and the country today that unless they take the other three steps, and do it soon, they will continue unable to make what is physically possible in this glorious country of ours actually financially possible for the people who live in the country. They will thus be constantly in danger of deflation or depression and of dangerous rises in price.
