I wish to make one or two observations on this section. This after all raises the question which has been raised by the hon. member for Lethbridge as to whether or not there should

be any attempt to impose a check of any kind on the credit-issuing power of the financial authority.
Under the Bank of Canada Act it was provided that the bank should have a 25 per cent reserve against its notgs and deposit liabilities. That was changed early in the war because it was felt at that time that it would be desirable to mobilize all our resources of gold and United States dollars in the hands of the foreign exchange control board for the purpose of protecting the position of the Canadian dollar, which at that time had been given a fixed ratio to the United States dollar of 90 cents. When we had our dollar at a fixed ratio obviously it had to be supported, and sometimes it cost money to do it.
Those of us in this house will remember that in 1947 there was quite a loss to the fund. At that time it cost the foreign exchange control board over a billion dollars of its gold and United States funds to protect our dollar. There were differences of opinion at that time as to just what course should have been followed with regard to the Canadian dollar, but there is no need to take any of the time of the committee to consider that now.
In the discussion in the banking and commerce committee yesterday this point of a fixed reserve was raised, and I should like to put this discussion briefly on the record. There is of course the view which has been expressed in this house this afternoon that money should be entirely a managed thing, that there should be no attempt to impose a check of any kind. That was discussed in the committee yesterday, and I think it would be fair to say the view of the experts was that while at the present time they felt that it was wise to leave in abeyance clause 26 of the Bank of Canada Act-in other words they did not think it was wise to reimpose the requirement of 25 per cent gold backing of the currency-nevertheless they did not go the length of saying that a reserve check of some kind was an outmoded superstition.
I was very glad to hear that, because after all there is a view very strongly held that if the regulation of the currency has no check of any kind and is left merely to the government of the day, even governments, as good as they think they are, are composed of human beings, and it may possibly be that when a difficulty comes the desire to ease the situation by inflating the currency may prevail. I am not going to pursue this at length, but I do want to have it on the record that I think the question of a reserve of some kind, a check on the

purely managed currency, should not be regarded as an outworn superstition. I think it should be seriously considered. I am not going to ask the committee to spend time considering it this afternoon. I am anxious just to put it on the record.
The danger I am pointing out is that when money is left entirely to be managed, it may have the effect of our slipping into inflation. That is a real danger. On the other hand, of course it is difficult. The question of the fixed reserve is difficult. You can travesty it. You may say: are you going to set up some kind of fixed reserve requirement and then are you going to obey it? And is the fixed requirement which has been set up to have a higher power than those who set it up and who may feel at the moment that it would be well to cast it aside? That is an argument which is made against a fixed reserve. It is easy to make it. All I wish to do at the moment is say that I was glad to observe in the committee that the view, as far as I could ascertain, in the department was that for the moment in this troubled situation they felt it was wise, as they said, to mobilize all our resources of gold and United States dollars for the purpose of having it all available as a sort of reserve to prevent any violent fluctuations in the currency which at the present time, as you know, finds its own level in the open market.
While that was their present feeling there is the possibility that in more normal times, they would revert to the thinking which was prevalent at the time the Bank of Canada was set up, namely that it was wise to set up a requirement for a fixed reserve-a reserve which would be the result of the best thinking you could give to it in normal times, when you are able to study the matter out in the most well considered manner, so as to have that as a protection to the public against the time when perhaps under stress and strain and with all kinds of abnormal situations arising, the managers of the currency, if it was under no restriction of any kind, might be tempted to take actions which in their better moments they would not take. I think that is all I want to say.

May I say a further word in connection with this matter? One of the disconcerting facts about our whole financial set-up in Canada, a fact which is not provided against in this legislation, is that if a depression begins to come on us we have no device whatsoever whereby we can arrest the rapid withdrawal of loans by the banks and the consequent withdrawal from circulation of a large percentage of the money which the

nation simply has to have to carry on its business. That is the kind of thing that occurred during the great depression in Canada and the United States. The United States could not see how in the world to get back into circulation the $8 billion-one-third of their purchasing medium-which went out of circulation just as a result of the withdrawal of loans by banks and the neglect to advance further loans.
So far as the minister's financial set-up at the present time is concerned, I think he will agree with me, being a man of much experience in this respect, that if a depression began to come on us in Canada he would be at his wits' end to know how to stop the banks withdrawing loans and thereby aggravating the very condition which was beginning to come upon us. On occasions like that, Social Crediters maintain that the government can stop that withdrawing of loans if it wisely uses the technique of debt-free money created by the state and spent into circulation where necessary. This criticism of course applies right through this bill but, in my judgment, is particularly appropriate right at this very point.
I wish to make one further suggestion to the minister. I should like to refer him, as an illustration of the soundness of the policy that Social Crediters advocate and that I am advocating here, to the Finance Act of 1914, at the commencement of world war I, and the Finance Act of 1923 which was a sort of consolidation of the Finance Act of 1914 in the light of the experience our fathers had during the first great war. The Finance Act of 1914 gave the Minister of Finance authority to create dollar bills, two dollar bills, and spend them into circulation if he saw fit. That is to be found very definitely in the report of the royal commission on banking and currency published in 1933. All members can read about the whole matter and its effect on our financial life in paragraph 47 on page 22 of that report.
I should also like to recall to the minister the important fact that under the Finance Act of 1914 the treasury of Canada issued $50 million, bought $50 million worth of wheat in Canada and lent the wheat to Great Britain. There was no financial cost whatsoever. That transaction is also recorded in paragraph 47 on page 22 of the document to which I have referred. If the minister were clothed with that power today, which, by the way, was technically taken away when the Bank of Canada was established and the Finance Act of 1923 was repealed, he would be able to do remarkable things of value in respect of the Canadian economy which at the present time he would not be free to do. The

technique of debt-free money worked admirably on that occasion and it would work admirably today.
I suggest to the minister in all seriousness that he should have his department take steps to re-enact the Finance Act of 1923 with suitable changes or modifications that would naturally result from the experience we have had in finance since 1923. If he would do that this year he would prepare himself for dealing with several serious financial problems which are likely to present themselves to us. As an illustration, when the Minister of Agriculture was faced with the problem of supporting the prices of beef, mutton and pork in Canada just before and just after the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease, if the Minister of Finance had been armed with the Finance Act of 1923 he could have created debt-free money and purchased enough beef, pork and mutton from a sufficient number of packing plants to enable them to buy the surpluses going on the market in respect of these meats, and could have maintained the price level of meat in Canada without a ripple. He could have given that meat to Great Britain or lent it to her for ten or twenty years. He would have got it out of the Canadian economy and saved this nation hundreds of millions of dollars and a good many nights of headache for himself.
That is just how simple this thing is. It is exactly the same device that was used in world war I. If it could be used in world war I, when so many of the producers were fighting overseas and there was a natural tendency to scarcity of production, how much more successfully could it be used in 1952 when all over our economy we have a surplus of supply which is threatening a descent into a depression. I suggest that the Minister of Finance take under advisement immediately the feasibility of causing a revised version of the Finance Act of 1923 to be passed by the house. It would not displace the Bank of Canada. The Bank of Canada would go on financing consumption through loans as it now does. This other mechanism would enable the minister to create debt-free money and spend it into circulation financing consumption as the supply position in the nation justified such creation and expenditure.

Before we leave item 1 I should like to ask the Minister of Agriculture something about the progress of the South Saskatchewan dam. It seems to me this matter is being held up altogether too long.
I would like, as preparation for the questions I wish to ask about the dam, to recall to the minister something I am sure he knows-the general set-up in which this dam should be placed.
I am not sure that all members of the house today understand as they should, and as they would if they came from the west, the situation in which Saskatchewan and Alberta find themselves. In order to appreciate the situation and the urgent need for this dam it is important to know that in the three prairie provinces there is a wide area which normally has far too little rain. The result is that sometimes we have good crops and that most times we do not have good crops. Most times the climate is too dry to produce good crops. This great area, as the minister will recall, is named the Palliser triangle. For the sake of those in the house who have not had an opportunity to hear about the Palliser triangle may I tell them just how they can find how big an area it is on the map.
The Palliser triangle in Alberta starts roughly at Banff according to some authorities and runs to a point some 30 or 40 miles north of Calgary. Then it runs northeast in a jagged line to the North Saskatchewan river where it crosses the Saskatchewan-Alberta boundary. Then it runs northeast to the junction of the North and South Saskatchewan rivers, then south to about Humboldt, then east in a jagged line to the Manitoba border near Swan River, Manitoba. It runs south on the Manitoba-Saskatchewan border to near Roblin, Manitoba, then east to lake Manitoba; then from the southern tip of lake Manitoba east to Beausejour, Manitoba, and then south to the United States boundary.
May I say to the members of the house, for the minister's sake, that all those who wish to understand the problem that is Canada's in the west must familiarize themselves with the facts about that vast uncertain area. Those who would be fair to the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba when estimating their financial capacity must be aware of the effect that

Supply-Agriculture
vast area has had on their public lives in every aspect, and consequently upon their financial condition.
As I have been able to gather, this great Palliser triangle was recognized to be a dangerous area for settlement long, long ago. Captain Palliser between 1857 and 1860 took a trip across this area and reported that it was not suitable for settlement, except for ranches. Hind in 1860 submitted a similar report. Professor John Macoun in 1879 similarly reported, as did Commissioner French of the R.C.M.P. in 1874. A. P. Patrick in 1879, Montague Aldous in 1881 and William Ogilvie in 1881 submitted similar reports.
I have mentioned only a few of many men. The reason I do so is to enable the members of the house to comprehend how serious a blunder the federal government committed in the years from 1900 to 1911 when they permitted wholesale settlement of that area by people who came in all through the south because certain areas in certain years made the country look prosperous and very promising.
Just in a word or two further to indicate how well men should have known how dangerous it was to let a large population go into that area may I give you some figures covering rainfall. In Medicine Hat between 1883 and 1901 the average rainfall was 8-061 inches. It is recognized everywhere that it is just next to impossible to grow crops with less than 12 inches of rainfall a year. The average rainfall in Calgary between 1885 and 1901 was 8-271 inches and for Macleod between 1896 and 1901 it was 7-735 inches.
In connection with this South Saskatchewan dam we need to go back to the year 1934. Although the federal government had permitted a great many people to come in and settle all through that Palliser triangle they did not recognize that thereby they were creating an almost impossible problem for the people who were going to administer those areas in a local way in times to come. The federal government failed to realize the tremendous responsibility it unquestionably incurred in permitting that settlement. They did not do a thing to help rehabilitate that country, to reimburse the provinces for the damage done them, until 1934 when Right Hon. R. B. Bennett's government passed the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. The present minister, in my judgment, will go down in Canadian history as a man of understanding vision and great courage because he has taken the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and expanded its activities in every way.
As I understand it, and the minister will correct me if I am wrong, the proposed South
IMr. Blackmore.]
Saskatchewan dam is one part of a general program which the minister has designed as a means of combating this problem which has arisen in the Palliser triangle and of making up in some small measure for the losses inflicted upon Alberta and Saskatchewan through unwise federal policies of the past.
I would be glad if the minister would take enough time to lay out before the house and the country the general picture; and would he set the South Saskatchewan dam into that picture?

I should like, therefore, to make some general remarks concerning the discussion of the agriculture estimates. In the first place, I may say it is a rather new experience to have the agriculture estimates coming in on the last day or two of the session. In the twenty sessions I have been here it has been customary to introduce the agriculture estimates at the first or almost the first of the session, I suppose because the word "agriculture" begins with the first letter of the alphabet. The discussion on these estimates usually takes place during the session and is completed on the last day or two of the session. But on this occasion we are introducing the estimates for the first time today.
I think that is largely due to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that on the first day of this session we found it necessary to introduce a special bill which made it possible for us to discuss almost everything that had to do with the handling of farm products. We were talking about the marketing of livestock products of all kinds. From that time until now we have been discussing, either in the house or in committee, those matters which we usually

discuss at the beginning of the session. I hope it will not be necessary, therefore, to give as full consideration to some matters at this time as it might otherwise have been.
I wish to point out at this stage that the total estimates for this year, as indicated in the main estimates, amount to $60,168,475, which is just $7,373,438 less than the total estimates for last year. We are now in a position to do what we have not usually been in a position to do when we introduce the agriculture estimates, in that we have the supplementaries before us. Those supple-mentaries amount to $14,379,042. When that amount is added to the main estimates, the total amount is considerably more than the estimates for last year. In going through the estimates from end to end, I think it will be found that a considerable part of that increase is due to the increases in salaries which have been made. Some of the increase is associated with the fact that we have undertaken to pay the freight on feed grain again this year, and the amount in the estimates this year for that purpose is more than a million dollars higher than it was last year.
There are other items which we will come to as we go through the estimates which will account for any increases which have been made, but generally speaking it was our intention this year to hold the estimates at about the same level as a year ago. The difficulties which have arisen as a result of certain diseases afflicting our livestock have made it necessary for us to change the items somewhat to provide more money in certain directions. Nevertheless the general objective was to have the estimates this year about the same as a year ago.
Some of the discussion which has taken place up to the present time in connection with agriculture has led me to give some thought, in the early stages of the discussion of these estimates, to the surpluses we have had in Canada during the past year. Those surpluses are pretty well limited to our exports. I have before me a table of the value of agricultural exports. It does not exactly indicate the volume of the different commodities, [DOT] whether they have increased or decreased, but generally speaking the fact that there have been increases does indicate that there has been an increase in the quantity as well as an increase in the price.
In order to place the picture before the house with regard to surpluses, I should like to point out that the total exports of farm products in 1951 amounted to $1,018,644,000. Out of that total, $950 million is accounted for through the export of grains and fodder and the export of animals and animal products. The first accounts for $735 million,

that is grain and fodder, which only leaves $215 million to be accounted for by all the livestock and livestock products exported. This only leaves $68 million to cover all other exports. It is correct to say, therefore, that in so far as exports are concerned they are related largely to our cereals, our grains and our livestock products. I suppose I could even go further and say that by far the greater part of the production on our farms is related to the same commodities.
I wanted to say that in the beginning in order to emphasize this fact, that the federal department has not had any troublesome surpluses during 1951 or 1952 down to the present. The main trouble we had with our wheat had to do in the first place with the wheat that we were carrying over from 1950, which was largely a frozen commodity and therefore had to be sold as feed whereas we are accustomed to selling it as human food. Last year our main difficulty was the season during which we had to harvest our grain crops in the western part of Canada. It was a wet season, and we found it most difficult to have our commodity harvested and stored in the usual manner and at the usual time but we did not experience any real difficulty in finding a place to market it, that is other than the difficulty that arose through the fact that it was frozen and was feed instead of being a commodity which human beings could consume. My information is that in due course we will succeed in having all that commodity marketed. I think we are having exactly the same experience we had in 1928 when we had a frozen crop. It is taking us about two years to market the crop as feed, whereas we would have counted on marketing it in one year as a commodity to be consumed by human beings.
Apart from that difficulty, we have not had any serious difficulty in finding markets. So far as the other farm products are concerned, the big one is cattle. We had a very ready market throughout all 1951 for our cattle. Fortunately we were marketing them at the highest price at which we have ever marketed cattle. That market was to be found in the United States. We marketed some
404,000	head of cattle either as live animals or as processed meat in some form or other. Therefore no difficulty was experienced in connection with the marketing of our cattle. Again, no difficulty was experienced in connection with the marketing of our hogs. A moment ago I stated that we marketed our cattle and beef at a comparatively high price, as compared with other years, in the United States. However, we marketed practically all our hogs in Canada. Throughout the whole of 1951 we marketed our hogs in Canada at

a higher price than that which United States farmers were obtaining for hogs in that country. The point I wish to make is that we have not been in the position in which we have had to make any complaint about the fact that we were not able to market our staple commodities other than wheat in Great Britain.
During last year and during the early part of this season we have heard comments to the effect that we were suffering because of the fact that we have not a market in the United Kingdom at present, or did not have such a market throughout 1951. I just wish to repeat that, with regard to cattle and hogs, we had a market for all those we produced throughout the year, and that we had a market at the highest price we have ever experienced for our livestock in any year in our history. The fact of the matter is that we were not experiencing any difficulty until the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic came upon us. For some little time after that occurrence we experienced some difficulties. Those difficulties were altogether associated with the fact that an embargo had been placed on livestock which prevented them from going across the United States boundary line. Our livestock and livestock products were therefore not permitted to cross the boundary. For a time we also had great difficulty in finding storage for the meat that was created by the number of animals which were coming on to the market.
We had about 33 per cent more hogs in 1952 than in the same period in 1951. Even if we had not had the foot-and-mouth disease epidemic, it is obvious that we would have had to seek markets other than those we had a year ago for hogs. The Canadian market would not have taken all of the hogs that came to market during the first three months of 1952.
The market we had counted upon was in the United States. We figured that we would be able to market about 50 million pounds of our pork products in that country. This quantity would not have gone to the United States in the form of live hogs because of the higher prices in Canada; at least not much

of it would have done so, if any. It would probably have gone in the form of cuts of pork. In the early part of the year the price for live hogs in Canada was higher than it was in the United States; but there were certain cuts of pork which could be sold in the United States at a higher level than that at which they could be sold in Canada. The reason for that is obvious. Their market is much greater than ours, and there is the possibility of selling foods of certain qualities at prices which are higher than those for which the same qualities of foods can be sold here. Whereas the whole hog would not bring as much money in the United States, there were parts of it which would bring more. We had a possible market in the United States for some 50 million pounds of those pork cuts. That market was, of course, shut off when the foot-and-mouth epidemic came upon us. That amount was all thrown back into our own market.
We have experienced more difficulty with that part of our surplus meat than with any other; and the dealing with it has been rather costly in the sense that we have had to put it in cans at costs which brought the price of the product to a figure which we cannot obtain in any part of the world that we know of. While we can sell some of it in the United States, we cannot sell it at a price representing the cost to us.
Time after time the statement has been made that this pork which has gone into cans has cost us about 64 cents a pound. I think the exact cost was 63-8 cents; and recently that figure has been reduced to 61-8 cents, which is about 2 cents lower. The costs are still going down slightly. But there is no place we know of where we can sell the commodity at that price. I am quite sure none of it can be sold in Canada at that price. I am also quite sure it cannot be sold at a price even approaching that figure in the United States. Nevertheless we have made up our minds that the commodity must be sold, and that the government will take some loss in connection with its sale. It is our intention and our hope to be able to put that commodity on the market either here or in the United States at ? fairly early date; and we will be putting forth an effort to put as much of it on that market as possible.
As to beef, in the beginning our difficulty was in getting rid of 'it at all. We had something in the neighbourhood of 400,000 head of cattle which might have come on the market in the twelve months of this year, to be sold somewhere outside Canada. Some of it had gone before the foot-and-mouth disease came upon us, but there would be at least 250,000 head of beef cattle to be sold

outside Canada during the remainder of this year after the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. We at once put forth an effort to find a place to put that meat. As has already been announced to the house, we finally found a market for it in Great Britain, through arrangements which we made with New Zealand and the United States. That meat is now going forward to that market. My information is that up to the present we have taken delivery of about 30 million pounds to be delivered under that arrangement, and that about half of it or a little better has already gone forward. The remainder is in position to be shipped from day to day to the British market.
This has resulted in the market pretty well adjusting itself to I think as favourable a position as any of us had any right to hope for, say a month or two months ago. During the last few days the market has been from a cent to two cents lower than it was when the foot-and-mouth epidemic came upon us. I repeat that that is a more fortunate position from the point of view of the producer than most of us anticipated at the time that situation developed.
The meat is moving out and the amount left on the market is not giving any serious trouble. I want to express the appreciation of those who have been attempting to meet a rather difficult situation to those who have been holding their cattle off the market. During the early stages at least 25 per cent of the cattle which usually come on the market were held off. That made it easier for those who were handling the problem while negotiating the contract which was eventually entered into with the British through contacts made with New Zealand and the United States.
We were asked at the beginning of the experience to place a floor price under cattle, and we did place a floor price of 25 cents under good steers basis Montreal and Toronto. It was suggested at the time that we should have set a price of 28i cents for choice steers, but we chose to set a floor price of 25 cents for good steers. I think I am correct in saying that a check of the market today will indicate that the price for choice steers is almost if not quite at the level that was asked for a month or a month and a half ago as a floor price.
I submit that it is better for everyone concerned that the difference between 25 cents for good steers and 28 or 29 cents which has been offered on the market in the last few years for choice steers should have resulted from activities on the market rather than from the government having
Supply-Agriculture
said, "Well, that is the price that is going to be assured; that is the price everyone is going to obtain." In any case we considered it better to have the price set, as we have set all floor prices that have been arranged, as a saviour against loss rather than as an incentive price which might bring about greater production of the commodity. So in setting it at 25 cents we put it on a basis for the time being which we considered would safeguard those who required to market their animals and make it possible at the same time to bring about a better price level if the marketing conditions warranted. I am pleased to note that the marketing conditions have warranted it, and the situation is going along much better than we anticipated it would at the time.
I do not think it is necessary for me to say any more at this time. As we go through the estimates and consider the different items I shall attempt to answer any questions which may be asked and give fuller information, both with regard to the matters I have been discussing and any others that may be brought up. In the meantime I ask the committee to consider these different items.

The report has been tabled and it deals with the administration of the Department of Agriculture. It continues:
Having considered the correspondence and records submitted together with the evidence adduced, your committee is of the opinion that the officials of the health of animals division, Department of Agriculture, followed the well defined plans laid down through long experience gained working in cooperation with their counterparts in the United States bureau of animal industry to diagnose and combat stomatitis and foot-and-mouth disease. As a result of this action, foot-and-mouth disease in Canada is definitely under control and appears to have been eradicated.
Your committee recognizes that it was and is most important that practices in Canada be similar to those in the United States so that Canadian livestock and other agricultural products may be permitted to re-enter the United States market at the earliest possible date, and commends the officials of the livestock branch. Department of Agriculture, for having adhered to those practices both with regard to diagnosing and combating the disease.
Your committee recommends continued and extensive research into all methods of diagnosis and control of animal contagious diseases in Canada.

All of which is respectfully submitted.
During the discussion an amendment was moved by the hon. member for Brant as follows:
Your committee is of the opinion that the evidence available to it discloses that there has been laxity and gross negligence with respect to the carrying out of the responsibilities of the office of the veterinary director general of Canada.
That the failure of the Minister of Agriculture to assure competent performance of duty by those responsible to him has cost the Canadian fanner a serious loss in export and domestic markets.
Your committee regrets the fact that the taking of evidence was restricted to federal government employees only and feels that the scope of the inquiry should have included independent witnesses from the area of foot-and-mouth infection.
Your committee strongly recommends the urgent need in the Department of Agriculture for greater co-operation between, and utilization of, facilities at its disposal for the diagnosis of animal diseases, and as evidence of the benefits to be derived by such co-operation would cite the excellent work accomplished since February 16, 1952, to eradicate this serious threat to the Canadian livestock industry.
I would point out that there was very little difference among members of the committee as to the manner in which this problem had been handled by the officials of the health of animals branch after February 18, but there was considerable difference of opinion as to how it had been handled from the first outbreak at the end of November and early December. Then many members of the committee were dissatisfied over the fact that we were not allowed to call independent witnesses who had first dealt with this outbreak, more particularly private veterinarians and certain R.C.M.P. officials.
Dr. Christie was before the committee on the last day, and although he had been in town several days we were allowed to question him for only two hours. The result was that many members did not have any opportunity to question Dr. Christie. It had also been agreed that certain other witnesses would be recalled, but that was not done. In my opinion there was considerable confusion as a result of the evidence we heard. A difference of opinion was expressed by certain veterinarians of the department, and in my opinion the investigation carried on by this committee was most unsatisfactory.
It was not a thorough investigation. As I say, several of the members desired to ask further questions of Dr. Christie but were not allowed to do so. It was my desire and the desire of other members that other witnesses should be recalled for further examination. Much of the evidence up to our last meeting could not be proved or disproved. There was a difference of opinion about there being gross negligence on the

part of the Department of Agriculture and the department of immigration.
It is only speculation, but it is thought that this disease was brought in from infected areas in Europe by an immigrant coming to this country. True enough this immigrant was brought to Hull once the disease was diagnosed and his clothing was tested, but that investigation did not prove or disprove anything at that date. This chap had been working on a farm in Germany where the entire herd was infected with foot-and-mouth disease. He then came to the Waas farm near Regina where the outbreak first occurred. There is a certain amount of circumstantial evidence as to where the disease came from. But as I say the investigation by the committee was such that many facts could not be proved or disproved.
No regulations were enforced to check immigrants from Mexico or other countries where this disease is so prevalent. I learned from questioning one of the veterinaries that since that date regulations have been put into force whereby immigrants coming to this country are now thoroughly checked, disinfected and so on to prevent the carriage of this dreaded virus into this country.
Much evidence was given as to what happened during December, January and past the middle of February. In my opinion there was carelessness on the part of the field supervisor in not issuing instructions and having them carried out during the months of December, January and the early part of February when new outbreaks of this dreaded disease occurred. Probably there is not much use crying over spilt milk, and no doubt it is only speculation to attempt to estimate what that carelessness during those three months has cost the cattle producers of this country.
True enough it is said that probably we were better off by the embargo riot being imposed earlier, but in my opinion the quicker this situation is cleared up the earlier the embargo will be lifted. Not even the minister can tell us when this embargo will be lifted. Under United States regulations a period of 60 days must elapse after the infestation is cleared up. Following our experience with the United States in past years, I believe there will be some trouble in having this embargo lifted before the 60 day period has elapsed.
It is certainly most important to the people of this country. Not only does it affect the western livestock producer; the cattle producers of the maritimes and eastern Canada have lost a wonderful market for their dairy cattle.

That is an all-time high as far as farm costs are concerned. In my opinion many farm costs are entirely too high, and I think the government has to assume some responsibility for that situation. In 1947, for instance, when the government was disposing of certain war assets, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture made representations to the government that they should retain one of the fertilizer plants built by the government during the war. We had some assurance from the then minister of reconstruction that one of those plants would be retained. However, they were both sold. At that time the figure we were given in the house as to the cost of production of fertilizer in the Calgary plant was $19 a ton. Today that same fertilizer is selling in western Canada at $106 a ton. I think that is entirely beyond reason, and if the minister wants to do a service to agriculture he should confer with the Minister of Justice and have the combines investigation people make some inquiry into why the farmers of this country have to pay the price they are paying for fertilizer today. I think it is entirely too high. I do not believe there is any reason for it being sold at that price, and I think it is essential that we have cheaper fertilizers in Canada, cheaper than we have had them up to the present time.
The minister has indicated that while we have large grain production our production of dairy products and of livestock in some cases has dropped seriously. I am sure that is not good as far as the agricultural industry in this country is concerned. If we are to have prosperous agriculture there has to be some greater production of the products which return something to the soil. One has only to look in eastern Canada at Ontario, Quebec, the maritimes, and see the number of abandoned farms, that fifty years ago supported families, raised families and educated families. Today they are abandoned and the same thing is occurring on a lesser scale in western Canada.
There again we find the policies followed by the government leading to the restriction of the products which would eventually

build up soil fertility and make for a more prosperous agriculture. I do not think it is good and I believe it is largely the result of the policy followed by the Minister of Agriculture over the last few years in failing to place reasonable floor prices under agricultural products. Not only has he failed to place these floor prices under agricultural products, decent prices from year to year; he has also failed to lay out any long term agricultural program as far as Canada is concerned. He has indicated that our market has been satisfactory. Well, I am saying to him that our market is not satisfactory at the present time.
If we are to have our maximum production of dairy products, of pork, of apples and of cheese, we must have a market for those products other than just our own Canadian market. The only other market I know of is the market in Great Britain. We have had no indication from the minister as to the permanent steps he or the government propose to take to get this market back and to keep it for us. We had a market there during the war. It was not expected by any of us that we could retain the complete market in Great Britain, but I do not think there was a farmer or anyone else in agriculture in this country who felt in 1945 that in two or three years we would have completely lost our market in Great Britain for dairy products, cheese, and apples. I would suggest to the minister that he give some indication to the house and the country of the permanent policy the government is going to follow to win back that market.

I should lilre also to ask the minister if he will give some further consideration to lowering the weight that

applies to the floor price for beef. I believe it is presently set at 500 pounds. I had several people come to me while I was in the west recently, showing me the returns they had received from baby beef. One man in particular had been approached by one of the shippers who was going to send a carload of beef to the Edmonton market. It was just after the floor price legislation had come into effect, and he was assured that the Edmonton market would absorb the shipment at a fair price.
This man shipped four baby beef to that market, and his net return was something in the neighbourhood of $337 after the freight and other expenses had been paid. He assured me that the year before he had shipped four animals of the same weight and quality and had received a return of something better than $1,000. That certainly does not represent a satisfactory marketing situation. I am told, and I believe from the reading of press reports, that the spreads between the various grades of beef and pork under the floor price legislation presently in effect are not working out to the advantage of many producers in this country. There is too great a spread between the grades under which the government has floor prices and some of the lower grades.
It is all right for the minister to say that no farmer should ship an animal until it reaches a certain weight, or that he should raise an animal which will make a certain grade. Unfortunately many of our farmers have not the right type of stock. While these spreads may be an incentive towards obtaining better stock, nevertheless there are some farmers in serious economic difficulties because of the failure of the government to establish reasonable spreads in the floor price legislation, and to see that the packers and others who are buying these products pay the farmers reasonable prices for the lower grades.

I was very interested in the speech the minister made before the recess, especially his reference to the fact that in

1951 we had been able to market our farm products at fairly satisfactory prices. I am wondering what the prospect is for the immediate future, because I recall that when the minister spoke before the food and agriculture organization he stressed the fact that we had quite large supplies of feed grain on hand and we were, therefore, in a position to expand our production of livestock. On the other hand the minister did not think the farmers would be likely to expand the production of livestock unless they had greater assurance with regard to markets for that increased production.
Then when the minister spoke before the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in reply to certain questions he pointed out that Britain lacked the dollars to buy our pork, cheese and eggs, and therefore he was not going to ask any farmer to expand his production of those products. There is no doubt that we could expand our production of livestock, cheese and various other commodities. There is no doubt that there is a very real need for that increased production in the world today. We have been told time and again by the officials of the FAO and other bodies about the urgent need for food. We have been told by the Secretary of State for External Affairs about the need for food. It is not very satisfactory, therefore, for us to have to say to our farmers that we are not going to ask them to expand production of food because if they do there may not be a market for it.
It is not good enough to say that we can market the food we are producing. The question is, can we expand our production so as to produce all the food we can, and if we do will there be a market for it? I saw an article in the Albertan which stated that the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had asked for a food plan which would make it possible to get the surplus to the needy nations. Reference was made to the fact that the international commodity clearing house idea had collapsed as a result of many nations not being prepared to support it. The federation also requested that some kind of board be set up to assure that if we expand production in this country there will be a market for our products.
What I should like to ask the minister is whether or not anything is now being done to set up the mechanism by which increased production of livestock could be marketed. I realize, of course, that the foot-and-mouth disease, for the time being, has made the problem more difficult, but the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture, to which I referred, was made before the out-

break of foot-and-mouth disease. Evidently, therefore, at that time-that is at the end of last year-he foresaw difficulty in marketing our farm produce. I can believe that this is not really a problem for the Minister of Agriculture. His main problem is to get production. The problem of marketing surpluses, I presume, rests with the Department of Trade and Commerce and more especially with the Minister of Finance, because the whole question of marketing our surpluses of farm produce is largely a monetary problem.
I do not doubt for one minute that if the Minister of Finance were to find ways and means of financing the sale of farm products to other countries, the Minister of Agriculture would be very pleased to see that that expanded production took place. I am wondering whether or not the Minister of Agriculture has received any assurance from his colleagues that if he tries to step up production of agricultural products in this country there will be a market for them.

I think I might say that does not apply to agricultural products alone but to some other things as well. It will be recalled that in this country we were producing at our peak in 1943 and 1944. I do not need to go over the quantities; they have been mentioned in this house so often one does not need to repeat them. Production was at the peak at that time.
The British took the trouble to send a man over here to tell us what was in store for us in the future. He went right across this country and appeared at every farm organization meeting that was held. I appeared with him in Regina and listened to what he had to say. He told us definitely that we would not be able to sell the quantity of bacon that we were then selling in Britain once the war was over. He told us the reasons for that. He said that when the war was over Britain was going back to trading bicycles, for example, for certain products in Denmark. He used that as one illustration, and went on to point out that they had made definite agreements following the 1932 conference here in Ottawa concerning what they were to buy from other countries, not only before the war but afterward. We are going along as best we can under that arrangement now. These agreements have been re-established with all the countries in

the world, from which Britain gets food. She has not established any position with us in relation to food.
What I said this afternoon was that we had no great complaint to make because during part of the time we had been able to sell in the United States all the beef we did produce, and for twice as much as we could get for it in Britain, and we have been able to sell in Canada all of the hogs we have produced. I do not say "all we could have produced". What I say is that we have sold all that we have produced in Canada at a higher price than we could in the United States. It was suggested a moment ago that the problem of marketing farm products is the responsibility of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. That statement is not true at all times. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has nothing whatever to do with the marketing of farm products in Canada. That is not trade and commerce.

Mr. Chairman, as this is my first opportunity to address this honourable chamber, and as it is my privilege to speak in my native tongue, I propose to speak in the French language.
(Translation):
Agriculture being the most important industry in the constituency I have the privilege to represent in this house, I wish, Mr. Chairman, to make a few remarks in connection with the debate which is now taking place on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, whose responsibility it is to find! markets for our farm products, and if need be, to grant subsidies in order to fill the existing gap between the present sale price of these products and the processing or production costs.
We are now faced, in certain districts of the province of Quebec, particularly in my own district, with a rather awkward situation. While the civil and religious authorities encourage my compatriots to settle on farms; while the provincial authorities spend large amounts of money in order to facilitate their establishment in new areas; while those same authorities make considerable efforts to open new districts to colonization and agriculture, it so happens that those who are already

settled on farms, those who derive their livelihood from the soil, have in the past six months been going through a period of very-alarming difficulties. There seems to be no solution in sight without prompt and efficient action on the part of the Department of Agriculture.
I have no intention, Mr. Chairman, of turning this speech into a plea for agriculture. I would nevertheless like to say that this branch of our economic life has always been and always will be our society's basic industry. When agriculture is prosperous, the workers' position in the towns is improved. Other classes are equally better off for it. A large number of industries are dependent upon agriculture. These are processing industries, manufacturing industries for equipment used in agriculture, transport companies and a great many others.
The agricultural industry deserves our particular attention for another reason.
Let us not forget that the agricultural worker is among those whose professions are exceedingly hard and risky. We all know that the agricultural profession does not lead to a quick fortune. It requires solitude, long working hours from the crack of dawn to sunset. It does not afford the pleasures and comfort of the big city; even holidays are denied to the farmer and on Sundays he still has work to do.
In order to succeed, the farmer must call upon the help of his entire family, regardless of age or even sex. The mother herself must do her bit on the farm, besides her household chores. Many a farmer has told me that he would never have mustered enough courage to remain on his farm had it not been for the heroic help of his wife; and yet, in spite of the concerted efforts of the whole family, the farmer's income is uncertain, for he is at the mercy of the weather, rain, drought, frost, hail, as well as of economic conditions.
Mr. Chairman, when members of a social class as important as our farming class willingly accept such sacrifices in order to achieve success the leaders are duty bound, I think, to grant them very special consideration.
I want to point out that during the last war, when the forces of evil represented by the fascist dictatorship were struggling against the forces of light for which we stood, our farmers and dairymen were called upon to sell their products such as cheese, butter, eggs and bacon at prices they considered inadequate. They willingly made the sacrifices known to the hon. members of the house. They readily agreed to them not only because they understood that they were
Supply-Agriculture
sacrificing themselves to a noble cause but because they were confident that the countries which they had helped to save from starvation would, once victory had been won, recognize their indebtedness and continue to buy our agricultural products even if, owing to somewhat different economic conditions, our producers were compelled to sell these products at a slightly higher price.
As a result of production costs today and the closing of foreign markets, our farmers are suffering serious losses in the marketing of their products, ranging from 10 to 25 per cent.
In support of this statement, I would like to read, if I may, a letter I have received recently from a farmers' co-operative of my county. I shall dispense with the congratulations the letter has for me since I presume they would be of no interest to the majority of this house. I quote:
Chambord, May 31, 1952
Mr. Paul Spence,
Member of Parliament for Roberval,
Mistassini, P.Q.
During your electoral campaign, you probably came to realize how very precarious is the marketing situation for our products, and for cheese especially, which is not selling at all. However, la Federee is reported to have succeeded in making a sale this week at 27 cents. This price is still much below production costs in view of the price of farm machinery, feed and labour.
Computations have been made, and at $4 a hundredweight for milk, a farm must be well run if is going to yield its owner 50 cents an hour. Moreover, in our district, where almost the entire production is converted into butter and cheese, the producer gets about $2.25 a hundredweight for milk; which is a starvation wage.
If the government fails to do something to raise the prices of agricultural products, the farmers will not be able to produce at a loss indefinitely; the result will be a shortage of foodstuffs which may produce many other shortages.
I am forwarding you a copy of a letter I sent this very day to the Minister of Agriculture; please read it and intercede on our behalf with the minister.
Yours truly,
Marie Brassard, secretary Co-operative Agricultural Society (S.C.A.) of Chambord-West
I now read the letter to which Miss Brassard has just referred:
Chambord, May 31, 1952.
The Hon. J. G. Gardiner,
Minister of Agriculture,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
I have been requested by the board of directors of the Chambord West Agricultural Co-operative Society, to inform you that the directors strongly

Supply-Agriculture
support the representations of the Catholic Farmers' Union (UCC) in connection with the decrease in the price of dairy products.
The situation greatly affects farmers of our district, since dairy farming is the basis of the agricultural industry.
The farmers' task is to produce and they are doing their duty, but they will be unable to keep on if they have to produce at a loss. There might be a shortage of foodstuffs then. It is your duty to prevent and avoid such a situation.
Respectfully yours,
Marie Brassard, secretary Chambord West Agricultural Co-operative Society.
Now, at Chambord, in the constituency of Roberval, dairy farmers, who must sell their milk at $4 per cwt. in order to earn a salary of 50 cents an hour, are receiving only $2.25. That means that not only do they not earn any salary at all, but that they are producing at a loss. Other important agricultural organizations have made representations to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).
Thus, on the 1st of June of this year, a Montreal newspaper, La Patrie, published an account of a meeting held at Sherbrooke, from which I want to quote a few excerpts which show clearly the deep feeling of apprehension and dissatisfaction which prevails among our agricultural class in the province of Quebec. I quote:
La Patrie
Sunday. June 1, 1952.
Sherbrooke-Thirteen hundred farmers from the eastern townships gathered in the parochial hall of the Immaculate Conception, have approved the following recommendations which have been forwarded to the federal Minister of Agriculture.
Whereas, out of sixteen billion pounds of milk produced in this country, six and a half billion, or 40 per cent, are made into butter; whereas in the province of Quebec alone butter production is the main source of income for 80,000 farmers out of 125,000, it is therefore resolved that a protest be registered against the Honourable J. G. Gardiner, federal Minister of Agriculture, who, on January 23, 1952, stated that "strictly speaking butter producers are not dairymen".
Whereas imported butter competes against our product and tends to reduce its price; whereas Canadian butter would be in a better position to meet this competition were not imported butter, whose flavour is different, "reprocessed" and mixed in with our own, it is therefore resolved that the government be requested to legislate so that any imported butter be sold unchanged in its original condition, and be so designated.
Whereas the price of cheese and butter affects the price of other dairy products; whereas we have imported 11,800,000 pounds of cheese at a time when it was to be expected that Great Britain would not renew her agreement with Canada; resolved that the federal government be asked to flx a support price of 30 cents per pound.
Whereas the western farmers are granted, under various forms, financial assistance of not less than $100 million by the dominion government, resolved: first, that federal members from eastern Canada be asked to defend our interests with an energy comparable to the energy shown by the western members in defence of their wheat producers; second, that
the Hon. Mr. Gardiner, federal Minister of Agriculture, be asked to show eastern farmers the same consideration as is given western farmers.
Mr. Chairman, the farmers in my province are under the impression that the Minister of Agriculture denies them the same measure of protection he extends to farmers in other parts of the country. They are not opposed, it is to be noted, to the assistance provided to the wheat producers of the western provinces. They only wish to receive the same consideration from government authorities. I support them in their view that part of the taxes they pay in order to cover the cost of administration of this country be returned to them under the form of financial assistance or subsidies when lack of foresight on the part of the leaders of the country is the cause of a crisis in the field of marketing such as the one the farmers are now undergoing.
The farmers in my riding are so dissatisfied that they chose to express their dissatisfaction in no uncertain terms, a few weeks ago. That is why they have sent me here to protest against the neglectful manner in which they are treated by the government. I wish to point out, by way of digression, that I would have obtained a larger majority if I had been faced only with the official candidate because nearly three quarters of the supporters of the independent candidate profess the same feelings as my own supporters.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few words to say and suggestions to make to the Minister of Agriculture. We have heard rumours that there is a possibility of losing the great experimental farm here in Ottawa. I would be absolutely opposed to that farm being given up to any housing project. Not only are the people of Ottawa and those who live in the immediate vicinity proud of this farm; it is worthy of the pride of all Canadians. I am sure if the farm were advertised more it would be a great attraction to United States visitors.
Recently we were invited by the Halifax board of trade to visit that city and on that trip I saw the damage that has been caused by the tides. If this condition is allowed to continue over the years many acres of land will be lost. They are trying to protect this land now, but if other means are not adopted it will all be washed into the sea. Cement walls should be erected near the mouths of these washes which have been caused by tidal action so this land may be saved. If a little country like Holland can keep out the sea in order to protect its farmland, we in Canada can do the same thing.
A great deal has been said about the high prices of farm machinery. I submit that a full-scale investigation should be held to see whether these prices are out of line with the prices of farm products. They are certainly out of line with the prices of some farm products. If such an investigation were held and it was found that there was no reason to reduce the prices of farm machinery, our farmers would be satisfied. Certainly at the present time when you go in to have a small repair done on a piece of machinery you find that it runs into many dollars. Many types
Supply-Agriculture
of farm machinery are being sold in the United States at much lower prices than they can be obtained for in Canada.
Reference has been made to the cost of fertilizer. I shall not elaborate on that because we all know how high it is. But I think something should be done about the prices of commercial feeds, such as hog starter, chicken starter, turkey starter, laying mash and calf meal. All these feeds are very high in price. Farmers are getting as low as 18 cents per dozen for eggs, and many of them are wondering whether they should stay in business. I was talking to some folks a week or two ago, and they told me they had sold all their chickens because they were not making money.
There should be a proper floor price under eggs. I was talking to a poultry inspector, and he told me the producers are not getting sufficient benefit from the floor prices. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will dig into this a little more and develop something which will enable these chicken raisers to stay in business.
I am told that our farmers would like to see the floor prices on cattle applied to the lower weights. I understand that with an animal weighing 500 pounds the floor prices do not apply, and that some have been selling calves for as low as 10 or 12 cents a pound. If the floor prices were applied to the lower grades it would help the farming community.
I think the revolving fund should be used to a greater extent. The drain on agricultural labour has been considerable because of recruitment into the armed forces and the young people who are leaving the farm to work in defence industry. The farmers are finding the cost of labour so high they cannot meet it with the prices they are receiving for what they produce. If this revolving fund were used to a greater extent it would help to keep the boys and girls on the farm and thus make possible a greater agricultural production.
Anyone who has not lived on a farm cannot realize how parents are worrying today. I know one farmer with a son about 17 or 18 years of age. That boy does not want to stay on the farm at any price. He claims he can go to the city and get good wages in an industrial plant, along with three weeks' holidays with pay, sick leave, other holidays and no work on Saturdays or Sundays. That is why 20 per cent of the population of Canada are drifting into the cities. This situation must be rectified even though it costs $200 million or $500 million.

Supply-Agriculture
This trend is noticeable all through Canada. If the government will take the necessary steps to correct this situation, not only will the people on the farm be benefited; it will benefit those who live in the cities, because these farm boys and girls are coming to the cities to steal their jobs. Every possible means should be adopted to keep the boys and girls on the farm.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to
take only a few minutes because, as the Minister of Agriculture has said, this department has been discussed on many occasions since the present session started. Certain elections have also provided an opportunity to discuss these matters, even though that discussion did not take place here. Therefore I am not going to take much time tonight. I was glad to hear the minister state at the beginning of his address that A stands for agriculture and that his department is usually discussed first when estimates are under consideration. He should perhaps have gone further and stated that agriculture is our first and basic industry. I think it is now recognized by people all over Canada that without a prosperous agriculture we cannot have a prosperous Canada. It is in the interests of labour, organized and unorganized, to see that agriculture is kept in a prosperous condition. Otherwise they will have difficulty finding markets for the things they produce and without the production of which they cannot have employment.
We have heard many statements over the radio, have seen them in the press and have also heard politicians say that agriculture is in a very prosperous condition at the present time. I am not ready to agree entirely. Figures given us by the bureau of statistics a few months ago show that a little over 20 per cent of the population of Canada live on farms and receive only 9-95 per cent of the national income. In my opinion that is not sufficient compensation for those who work on the land. If farmers go ahead and produce a lot, as they are at all times willing to do, then they find they are cutting each other's throat because of a lack of markets, and the prices of their products go down.
So far as secondary industries are concerned, all they have to do is close their factories for a while, let their stocks go down and create a shortage. If the farmers were to do that by going on strike we would immediately have an outcry against them. A few weeks ago I had a letter from one of my constituents at Dewberry, Alberta. It is
[Mr. Sinnott.l
dated May 17, 1952, and is addressed to myself at the House of Commons. It is written by a storekeeper for one of the farmers in the district. The letter reads:

I just want to say this, Mr. Chairman. If putting the facts before the taxpayers of this country is playing politics, I am going to be playing politics as long as I sit in this House of Commons. Certainly that is all this party has ever tried to do, to place the facts before the public and let them know just what did happen.
This afternoon the hon. member for Souris read the report of this committee. I intend to repeat only that part of it which is so important. It is the second paragraph, and reads as follows:
Having considered the correspondence and records submitted together with the evidence adduced, your committee is of the opinion that the officials of the health of animals division. Department of Agriculture, followed the well defined plans laid down through long experience gained working in cooperation with their counterparts in the United States bureau of animal industry to diagnose and combat stomatitis and foot-and-mouth disease.
In the first place, Mr. Chairman, it has never been proven that stomatitis did exist. Of course, on the other hand, it has never been proven that it did not exist; I must be lair. But why did stomatitis have to appear in that report? It was to cover up. It is stated in the report that the department followed the well-defined plans laid down through
Supply-Agriculture
long experience gained working in co-operation with their counterparts in the United States bureau of animal industry. I have here the 1942 year book on agriculture, "Keeping livestock healthy" put out by the United States department of agriculture. Speaking of foot-and-mouth disease at page 270, it says this; and I want to quote this complete paragraph:
In making a diagnosis the facts just discussed are used to determine which of the three diseases an infected animal has. The procedure is to inoculate swine, cattle, guinea pigs, and horses with material obtained from the sick animal. The diagnosis of foot-and-mouth disease is clear and can be made unhesitatingly if the typical vesicles, preceded by a rise in temperature, developed in all these animals except the horses. When all the injected animals including the horses develop vesicular lesions, the disease would be diagnosed as vesicular stomatitis. When lesions are produced in swine, less frequently and to a milder degree in horses, and not at all in cattle or guinea pigs, the condition is typical of vesicular exanthema of swine.
In view of the statement in the report that they had followed the well-defined plans as set out by the United States bureau of animal industry, and in view of the completely contradictory statement in this book which is sent out by the United States department of agriculture, I believe the report contains a misstatement of fact. In view of that, I certainly cannot agree with it.
As I mentioned before, I do not know why stomatitis was written into that report, other than to cover up, because some of the top officials insisted-I say "insisted" advisedly -that it was stomatitis. We had considerable evidence and a number of statements in the committee that it was important to follow the United States method of diagnosis. I am a good Canadian, Mr. Chairman, and I have so many times heard statements made about how much better the United States is than Canada. In many cases it may be true, but I do say that we have something in Canada that we are very proud of and should brag about. I hate to see it belittled all the time by the Department of Agriculture, and especially by the minister under whose department it comes. I am referring to the animal diseases laboratory in Hull. We have a lab there for the purpose of diagnosing animal diseases as well as human diseases. Why should we not use it? Why should we not be proud of the fact that we have it? On the last page of the last committee report the minister attempted, with one of the committee witnesses, to belittle the Hull laboratory.
Now, the disease was diagnosed in Hull, though the minister says not. It was diagnosed there probably more or less by accident. As I said before it has been the policy of the department, and especially of the minister,

Supply-Agriculture
to try to maintain that the procedure followed was the correct one, regardless of the accuracy of that statement. Later in the committee we found that the officials from Saskatchewan were told at the start by a private veterinarian that this disease could be foot-and-mouth disease. We realize, Mr. Chairman, as much as anyone that it is important not to throw around the term foot-and-mouth disease as if it were nothing at all. We realize the necessity for being a little bit discreet about the use of the term. The minister said something in the committee the other day-fortunately it is not in the record because I would hate to see it there-intimating that it was probably a good thing this disease had not been diagnosed for two and a half months, that we would have lost a great deal more had it been diagnosed at the proper time.
The men working in the field for the health of animals branch have taken a great deal of criticism. The veterinary profession as a whole has taken a great deal of criticism as a result of this foot-and-mouth episode. It is unfortunate that just because of the stubborn attitude of some of the top officials of the department-

In view of the very serious outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Europe early in the fall and the subsequent outbreak in Great Britain, it is my theory that the Department of Agriculture and the department of immigration should have taken cognizance of the fact and been guarding against the transportation of the disease here by way of immigrants or any other means by which it could be carried. Some people may have the mistaken idea that the disease can only be carried by livestock. Mr. Chairman, that is very wrong. It is not a proven fact, and could not be proven at the time the immigrant Willi Brunt jen was brought to Ottawa, but it is my personal opinion, whatever it may be worth, that there can be no doubt that is how the disease arrived in this country. Seventeen days from the time he was on a farm in Germany infected with that disease, he was on the Waas farm in the Regina area. Strangely enough, he had left the employ of Mr. Waas before the disease was recognized. In the committee reports at page 53 Dr. Childs, the veterinary director general, made a statement that in my estimation is rather peculiar.

I do not want to repeat too much, Mr. Chairman, but I want to bring this one paragraph before you:
We know right well how it would affect international trade and affect the whole national economy.
He is referring to foot-and-mouth disease. To continue:
We know that well. However we did not suspect there would be foot-and-mouth disease up there. It was absolutely preposterous-2,000 miles from anywhere that you would expect it. You would expect it at some of our coasts or at our quarantine stations, but not out there.
I think it is rather too bad the veterinary director general should make that statement, because in this day and age it is not preposterous to find any disease any place to which it can be carried by human beings.
As I have said before, we have not criticized anything that has taken place since the diagnosis was made. What we have criticized-and we feel that the criticism has later proved to be justified-is the lag in diagnosis of the disease. At page 92 of the reports of the committee we find that Mr. Wright apparently made a statement, and then the Minister of Agriculture made a statement of which I want to read just a part:
In this case, if there Is anything at all about it that one can criticize, it is that they did not make a proper diagnosis, a correct diagnosis, earlier. Now, that happens right along, both in the practice of medicine and in veterinary practice; but there might be some reason for criticism there, but if there is any reason for criticism it is just as much the business of the provincial department as it is of the federal.
The minister has admitted that there might be some criticism for lateness or delay in diagnosis. We are therefore together on that point. With regard to the statement that it is just as much the business of the provincial department as it is of the federal department, may I say it is absolutely incorrect. As the minister later admitted, the responsibility with respect to any contagious disease in Canada rests with the federal Department of Agriculture.
Another thing I should like to bring out is the fact that one or two of the witnesses before the committee were so sure it was vesicular stomatitis that they could not see the forest for the trees. At page 205 of the reports of the committee we have Dr. Childs giving evidence in reply to questions by Mr. Cardiff, and we find the following:
Q. Is that not similar to foot-and-mouth disease, very closely related to it? A. It has some similarity,
Q. Well, if you were not absolutely sure, would it not prompt you to take a test and be absolutely sure that you were dealing with a very contagious disease?

Here is Dr. Childs' answer.
A. I was satisfied that we were dealing with simple vesicular stomatitis or we certainly would have gone further, and quicker, with the tests.
Later on at page 267, in giving replies to questions asked by myself, as a matter of fact, Dr. James said this:
Q. And you injected the horses? A. Yes.
Q. So that you would have preferred to have been able to get young horses from premises away from those on which the infection was suspected? A. Yes. Dr. Christie mentioned that at one time; but the unfortunate fact was that we just thought it was stomatitis and not so very important and that was not done.
Then at page 273, in answer to questions by Mr. Wright, Dr. James said:
Q. It would not indicate anything more dangerous, that was not the reason why you inoculated the horses-to determine whether there was anything more dangerous than stomatitis? It was simply to determine whether there was stomatitis or not? A. It is a quite common thing.
Q. In other words, there was no discussion between yourself and Dr. Carlson and Dr. Christie as to the possibility of this being anything dangerous? This was the first field test that would be made? A. No, the idea was we agreed that to satisfy ourselves we would inoculate horses.
Q. To satisfy yourselves? A. That they had stomatitis. We could prove stomatitis by producing a reaction in the horses.
Then again at page 277 we And this in answer to questions by Mr. Harkness:
Q. The thing you wanted to establish by injecting these horses was that it was stomatitis but, if it were not stomatitis it must have been in your mind that it was foot-and-mouth disease? A. No, it was not.
Q. Why inject the horses at all if you were certain it was stomatitis? A. Well, when you are sending an official document down to the head of government you do not want to play around with it. You want to have something to show you know what you are doing-to back up your judgment. To back up my judgment I inoculated the horses with the advice and instructions of my superior officers-not to satisfy myself about foot-and-mouth disease.
Earlier, in answer to a question by Mr. Harkness we find this:
Q. If you were not suspicious why did you inject these horses on December 3? A. To satisfy myself as to the type of virus we had.
Q. Is it true that the only thing an injection on the horses will do is to satisfy you that it is stomatitis or foot-and-mouth disease? A. I was not bothered about foot-and-mouth disease. I wanted to satisfy myself that we had stomatitis.
That is the evidence given by one of the veterinarians who appeared before the committee. Again at page 335 we have this evidence given by the assistant veterinary director general, Dr. Hall, in reply to questions by myself?
Q. And when you speak of a vesicular disease the first thing that comes to your mind is that it might be foot-and-mouth disease, is it not? A. Yes.
Q. Dr. Childs went out there on the 14th and he assured you; how could he be so sure that it was nothing else but stomatitis although he did not say

it was-of course, you cannot answer that-after he had been out did he state to you any reason for saying he was so sure it was stomatitis? A. I believe that was due to the fact that he had been in the stomatitis outbreak in 1938 and 1939; he had dealt with stomatitis.
Q. He had dealt with stomatitis? A. With stomatitis, more than I ever had.
Q. But he had not been out and seen this? A. He went there.
Q. But he did assure you that it was stomatitis and there was nothing to worry about? A. Nothing to worry about, that is correct.

Vesicular diseases are treacherous and the only sensible thing was to get specimens in as soon as possible and because we have a virus unit all the necessary work can be done perfectly safely. As I said before, the field tests as carried out were not, as is stated in the committee report, in accordance with the procedure in the United States. Three tests were made previous to February 18; two horses were injected on December 2, one horse was injected on December 12 and one on February 12. Of those four horses, one alone reacted to the test. That in itself should have been sufficient evidence to prove the existence of foot-and-mouth disease. In the case of the one horse which did react, it did not react until five days after the injection was made. I contend that it may not have been the injection that caused the vesicles, it may have been the toothbrush which they used to transfer the material. Almost anything could have happened.
One veterinarian was given the complete responsibility of making the injections and reading the results. I contend that is a dangerous procedure. No matter how good the veterinarian is I do not think he would want to have that responsibility. He would want somebody else along to consult with and to see that the work was done in accordance with the principle that two heads are better than one. However, that was not done.
