Injections were made into two each of young cattle, pigs, and horses in the presence of the veterinary director general.

Mr. Chairman, I do not think it is right or proper to let this pass. We have in this country a billion dollar industry, a livestock industry that is one of the greatest in the world. It is an industry that has taken a lot of time, hard work and trouble to get to the position it is in today. In Canada we have 8 million cattle. When you come to consider it, 8 million cattle in this country have to suffer because of the things that have happened in this house during the last three or four months. Three or four members of that committee-one of them more especially, though I do not blame him so much as he is a lawyer and I cannot say he should understand the cattle business

made definite statements, and they knew what harm they were doing to the cattle industry.
Let us take this episode tonight. What has happened? Tomorrow morning or tomorrow at noon the United States press will come out with this story of what has happened here tonight. If a man there is interested in cattle, what will he immediately do? His fears will be aroused at once. He will say: They've still got that disease up in Canada; they are still fighting over it.
Mr. Chairman, I think it has gone beyond all common sense and all reason to think that a member would get up in this house here and discuss this after it has all been talked over in the committee. I am sure if the

If there is anything that has done harm to the cattle business it has been this long weary talk about what is going on in the Regina district. In thinking about the diagnosis of these cases out in Regina I want to commend the veterinary department. They gathered seven veterinaries together. Those seven veterinaries went out to the Waas farm and looked it all over. Not one said there was foot-and-mouth disease. Those seven men kept track all the way through.
I will agree that hindsight is always better than foresight, and of course the hon member for Brant-Wentworth has had lots of hindsight. But he did not have much foresight, because if he had the foresight and the ability he says he had he would have flown out there and told them it was foot-and-mouth disease. He did not do that, but he started on a political proposition. He started it in the house, and then he started it in the committee. That is what we have had to put up with. The cattle industry in Canada, a real industry and the second largest in Canada, has had to put up with this kind of nonsense.
If you want to look the situation over what do you find? You find that they have had to kill thousands and thousands of cattle in the old country. They slaughter thousands of them, and you do not see one word about it in the press. All you see is that they have slaughtered cattle. They do not have it in committees, they never have arguments in the house, but we have had one or two men in this house trying to condemn our veterinarians who are doing their best. They have done their best; they say they are satisfied that they have cleaned it up; and they have done what they should have done since the 18th of February. Why can't these hon. members say they did a good job before that and help the industry out?
I say to this house and to the people of Canada that I know quite a lot about livestock; and I say the veterinarians did a thorough job all the way through, a thorough job. In the first place they did not let us down by crying "foot-and-mouth disease!" before they were absolutely sure. In the second place they carried on and they left the disease in such a way that they could

handle it. They quarantined all around. They handled it, and they proved that they have handled it. They also proved that they knew their job. I want to say to the member who has just spoken that whether he thinks so or not, and whether he likes it or not, we were very, very fortunate that the disease was in a very weakened condition and that those men did not find it as quickly as they might have found it if it had been stronger. If it had been as strong in the early part of November and December as it was in February they would have found it at first; but let me tell him that we would have still had the cattle we exported at that time. We would have lost the millions and millions of dollars that came from the United States for those cattle. I want to say we should be thankful that it was in that condition. After all, I am sure a lot of the hon. members know that in that part of the country it is the middle of May before the frost goes out of the ground, and quite often it will be June before all the ice goes. It was easy enough to say it was impossible to get that cleaned up. It is only now that they can say they are going at it in order to be sure that it is cleaned right up. They have put stock in there, and they are looking after it. I say in all sincerity and in all seriousness, for the betterment of the livestock industry of Canada, let us forget this thing. Let us leave it to those who know something about it. Let us carry on and help the trade, not hinder it.

ister during the months of November, December, January and up until February 15 or February 18. It seems fantastic to me that when a disease of this sort was detected it should not be reported immediately to the minister.
I confess that I am no farmer, as I said in the beginning, but I did do some research on the law relating to this subject. I looked up the original act, and it was the intention of the legislature that the minister should be informed right away. It was a matter of high policy as to how the disease should be dealt with. It should not be left to any minor official in the Department of Agriculture.
It was brought out in evidence that the veterinary director general maintained that he did the right thing in not reporting this and not having a diagnosis made in Hull. And the minister says, "We do not talk of foot-and-mouth disease; we do not mention it. Yet the fact is that in every report of the veterinary director general, and I looked at them for several years back, he is always reminding the veterinary doctors in the country to be on the watch for foot-and-mouth disease because there is nothing so dangerous for cattle.
In the face of that evidence it seems to me there is something to be said against the officials of the department. They did not take advantage of the facilities that were at their disposal; and indeed they may be considered to be negligent, as the opposition contended in the minority report.
